title: Redefining intranasal brain delivery: from nasal entry to meaningful parenchymal and cellular exposure

paragraphs.en: Recent global burden analyzes indicate that neurological conditions are now the leading cause of illness and disability, affecting more than three billion people globally (Steinmetz et al., 2024). Despite this substantial disease burden, therapeutic progress in central nervous system (CNS) disorders remains limited. A fundamental challenge lies in the difficulty of achieving sufficient and reproducible delivery of therapeutics to diseased brain regions. In particular, the blood–brain barrier (BBB) restricts the entry of over 98% of small-molecule drugs and virtually all macromolecular therapeutics, preventing many promising candidates from translating into effective CNS therapies (Pardridge 2005; Abbott et al. 2010). To bypass the BBB, invasive approaches such as intrathecal, intracerebroventricular, or convection-enhanced delivery are considered. However, their broader clinical use is constrained by procedural complexity, brain tissue injury, and the risk of infection (Lonser et al. 2015). To this end, nose-to-brain (N2B) delivery has emerged as a noninvasive approach with the potential to circumvent the BBB and offer broader clinical applicability and safer therapeutic access to the brain (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Wang et al. 2019; Keller et al. 2022).

The nasal route offers direct anatomical proximity to the CNS via neuroepithelial interfaces, avoids first-pass metabolism, and enables relatively rapid access to CNS-associated compartments (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Wang et al. 2019). Accordingly, interest in N2B delivery has expanded beyond small molecules to include peptides, proteins, antibodies, nucleic acids, and viral or virus-inspired delivery systems (Keller et al. 2022; Chung et al. 2023; Drath et al. 2025).

However, the translational significance of N2B delivery should not be overestimated based solely on route attractiveness (Yokel 2022). Clinically, approved intranasal CNS-related therapies remain largely limited to specific indications, such as treatment-resistant depression or seizure rescue, rather than serving as broadly applicable disease-modifying platforms (Higdon and Sperling 2021; Vasiliu 2023). This highlights a persistent gap between conceptual promise and mechanistically validated CNS delivery.

The imbalance in N2B delivery research arises from two fundamental issues in how the current research evaluates the delivery process. First, oversimplification of complexity of the delivery process to a single step process needs to be differentiated (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Wang et al. 2019; Yokel 2022). The assessment of the actual transport and tissue penetration processes following entry into the CNS is critical as cargo must not only cross the initial barriers but also traverse a complex sequence of physiological bottlenecks from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) turnover and perivascular constraints to the dense extracellular matrix (Iliff et al. 2012; Xie et al. 2013; Spera et al. 2023). Second, equating simple CNS exposure with successful delivery can lead to inaccurate interpretation of delivery outcomes (Ahmad et al. 2017; Yokel 2022). Relying on crude metrics like total brain uptake fails to distinguish whether a therapeutic has penetrated the target tissue or is trapped in non-target compartments, such as the CSF or meninges (Lochhead et al. 2015; Ahmad et al. 2017; Lochhead and Davis 2019). Moreover, this superficial metric provides no evidence of whether the therapeutic has achieved functional engagement with the target cells.

In this context, the present review aims to propose a stage-resolved mechanistic and evaluative framework for N2B delivery (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Wang et al. 2019; Yokel 2022). Specifically, we reconceptualize the N2B pathway as a sequence of transport stages and associated bottlenecks, extending from nasal entry to meaningful parenchymal and cellular access. We further examine the current imbalance in the field, whereby early nasal barriers have been extensively studied, whereas post-entry transport and tissue-access processes remain comparatively under-integrated in both mechanistic discussion and experimental validation (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Wang et al. 2019; Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025). On this basis, we systematize the validation criteria required at each stage of delivery and thereby propose an evaluative framework capable of distinguishing meaningful delivery from simple exposure (Lochhead et al. 2015; Ahmad et al. 2017; Yokel 2022). Finally, we discuss how formulation design may need to evolve beyond single-barrier optimization toward multistage-aware, disease-informed, and cargo-informed strategies.

Collectively, this perspective seeks to redefine N2B delivery not as a simple brain-uptake outcome, but as a sequential transport process that must be resolved across anatomical compartments and biological scales to achieve meaningful therapeutic impact.

sections.title: Intranasal delivery routes and stage-specific bottlenecks

paragraphs.en: Efficient N2B delivery is determined by initial events within the nasal cavity. Accordingly, the proportion of the therapeutic agent deposited and retained within the nasal microenvironment, rather than the administered dose, is a key factor for effective N2B delivery (Illum 2000; Kimbell et al. 2007; Foo et al. 2007; Djupesland 2013; Gao et al. 2020; Seifelnasr et al. 2024). However, effective deposition in the olfactory region can be primarily hindered by the anatomical complexity inherent within the nasal cavity. The olfactory region, a primary target for N2B transport, is located in the superior-posterior nasal cavity and is difficult to access (Illum 2000; Djupesland 2013). The anterior nasal architecture acts as an aerodynamic bottleneck where the narrow passages and complex geometry cause droplets to impact and become trapped before reaching the olfactory cleft. Indeed, conventional nasal sprays typically deliver less than 1% of the dose to the olfactory region (Figure 1) (Kimbell et al. 2007; Foo et al. 2007; Djupesland 2013; Gao et al. 2020; Seifelnasr et al. 2024).

Once a therapeutic cargo bypasses this stringent aerodynamic filter and deposits in the target region, it immediately encounters the mucosal interface. The nasal mucosal barrier is not a simple aqueous surface. It is a viscoelastic hydrogel network composed of mucin glycoproteins (Cone 2009; Boegh and Nielsen 2015). To cross this mucosal barrier and access underlying nasal epithelium, a therapeutic cargo must effectively penetrate this layer. Thus, successful delivery depends on balancing local retention with the ability to diffuse through the mucus mesh. Alongside this physical filter, mucociliary clearance (MCC) acts as the primary kinetic constraint, functioning as a physiological defense mechanism that rapidly clears administered therapeutics toward the nasopharynx (Gizurarson 1993; Merkus et al. 1998). While mucus interactions dictate the spatial mobility of a formulation, MCC imposes a strict temporal limit on these interactions. The outcome of this stage is fundamentally predicated on how long the cargo can reside within the mucus and how rapidly it can penetrate through it. Consequently, mucus architecture and MCC are functionally distinguished, but cooperatively control diffusion, local residence, and clearance (Gizurarson 1993; Merkus et al. 1998; Cone 2009; Boegh and Nielsen 2015).

This mechanistic link between formulation properties, deposition, and clearance was quantitatively established in research showing correlation of nasal clearance rates with formulation characteristics. Harris et al. demonstrated that increasing methylcellulose concentration increased the mean droplet size from approximately 51 to 81 μm and 200 μm, respectively, which exerted a non-linear effect on retention (Harris et al. 1988). Specifically, while the 0.25% methylcellulose formulation successfully prolonged nasal residence, the 0.50% formulation paradoxically accelerated clearance. Crucially, the same study revealed that increased viscosity shifted deposition further anteriorly. This highlights that local residence and regional deposition are not independently tunable variables but rather mechanistically coupled phenomena.

Beyond physical and kinetic barriers, delivery is further constrained by the local biochemical microenvironment. The nasal cavity typically maintains slightly acidic to near-neutral pH. These specific pH and ionic conditions can significantly alter the stability and ionization state of sensitive cargoes (Gizurarson 1993; Keller et al. 2022). Building on these chemical constraints, the nasal mucosa also functions as an ‘active metabolic barrier.’ It contains various enzyme systems, such as cytochrome P450 and glutathione S-transferases, which directly degrade therapeutics such as peptides, proteins, and nucleic acids (Longo et al. 1986; Baron et al. 1988; Aceto et al. 1989; Gervasi et al. 1991). Additionally, the mucosal immune barrier, consisting of secreted antibodies and innate defenses, introduces biological constraints that can limit delivery efficiency and reproducibility, particularly for viral vectors or repeated dosing. Ensuring the biological and physicochemical integrity of cargo within this environment is an absolute prerequisite upon entry into this hostile nasal environment.

In summary, the administered dose alone does not determine brain exposure. These compounded early-stage losses dictate the true functionally available fraction. Only the minor fraction of the cargo that successfully navigates these aerodynamic, kinetic, and physicochemical hurdles can proceed to the next obligatory step: epithelial crossing (Gao et al. 2020; Seifelnasr et al. 2024).

Once the therapeutic cargo breaches the superficial mucus layer, it immediately confronts the cellular front line, the nasal epithelium (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025; Qiu et al. 2025). It must cross the epithelial barrier to reach the lamina propria, thereby unlocking the downstream transport network. This critical stage marks the transition from surface exposure to true tissue penetration (Figure 2).

This epithelial crossing relies on two primary routes: extracellular and intracellular transport. Extracellular transport occurs via the paracellular route through the spaces between adjacent epithelial cells. However, this movement is immediately blocked by apical junctional complexes, specifically tight junctions. The dense network of transmembrane proteins like claudins and occludins seals the intercellular space into a formidable physical and electrostatic barrier. That resembles the molecular architecture found in the BBB (Steinke et al. 2008). The pore diameter of tight junctions in the nasal epithelium is approximately 0.4 to 0.8 nm, creating a size-exclusion threshold for passive paracellular diffusion (Sarin 2015). Consequently, these rigorous structural constraints ultimately restrict paracellular diffusion strictly to small (<1 kDa), hydrophilic solutes (Madara and Dharmsathaphorn 1985; Sarin 2015; Yokel 2022).

In contrast, the intracellular transport route can be further classified into two distinct pathways depending on the target cell type: epithelial transcellular passage and intraneuronal transport (Lin et al. 2016; Lochhead and Davis 2019; Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025; Qiu et al. 2025). The transcellular route, demanding direct migration of cargo through epithelial cells, incorporates transcellular transport via direct membrane passage and epithelial transcytosis via vesicle-mediated transport. Transcellular transport relies on passive partition and rapid intracellular diffusion, making it highly effective for small, lipophilic compounds (Illum 2000; Yokel 2022). In contrast, epithelial transcytosis is primarily utilized by larger biologics and nanoparticles to bypass tight junction limitations (Lin et al. 2016). Because this transcytotic pathway is an active biological process requiring sequential steps of apical uptake, intracellular routing, and basolateral release, it typically operates on a much longer timescale of tens of minutes to hours.

Further, intraneuronal transport implies entry into olfactory or trigeminal neurons followed by axonal transport (Buchner et al. 1987; Yokel 2022). The maximum rate of axonal transport in olfactory nerve C-fibers has been quantified at up to 130 mm/day (Buchner et al. 1987), taking at least 45 minutes for a substance to reach the rat brain after intranasal administration. This biological pathway cannot account for rapid CNS exposure due to its inherent slowness requiring hours to days in larger species. This is distinguished from other types of fluid flow, such as paracellular or perineural bulk flow pathways. These routes can bypass intracellular sorting networks entirely, allowing therapeutic cargoes to be detected in the brain and CSF within 5 to 10 minutes post-administration (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025; Qiu et al. 2025). Nevertheless, intraneuronal axonal transport can be an alternative route for delayed, sustained drug distribution.

Consequently, the rapid initial CNS exposure is mechanistically governed by paracellular penetration coupled with CSF-associated bulk flow, achieving within minutes of intranasal administration (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025; Qiu et al. 2025). While transcytosis may proceed concurrently, its slower kinetics make it a minor wave of entry rather than the primary driver of immediate brain exposure (Table 1).

Upon entering the lamina propria, nasal anatomical divergence directs the cargo along either olfactory or trigeminal nerve-associated compartments (Crowe and Hsu 2022; Qiu et al. 2025). Specifically, crossing the olfactory epithelium guides the cargo toward the olfactory nerve bundles. By contrast, entry through the respiratory epithelium offers access to the trigeminal nerve pathways, alongside local tissue retention or systemic absorption (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Crowe and Hsu 2022).

The spatial trajectory of the olfactory pathway requires cargoes to migrate alongside olfactory nerve bundles toward the cranial compartment (Renner et al. 2012; Norwood and Zhang, 2019). Importantly, the foramina of cribriform plate, densely packed with nerve fibers, blood vessels, and connective tissue, does not offer an unobstructed passageway. Because this dense anatomical arrangement drastically reduces the functionally available space, the cribriform plate acts as a highly restrictive physical bottleneck, forcing therapeutic cargoes to navigate through extremely narrow interstitial gaps to access the brain (Norwood and Zhang, 2019; Proulx 2021; Spera et al. 2023). Within this olfactory axis, transport mechanistically diverges into two distinct intraneuronal and extraneuronal pathways (Thorne et al. 2004; Renner et al. 2012; Drath et al. 2025). The intraneuronal route provides the advantage of direct delivery to the olfactory bulb, but its slow speed, restricted by motor protein velocities across microtubules, results in low efficiency. By contrast, extraneuronal pathways are closely coupled to the subarachnoid space (SAS) and CSF-associated compartments, facilitating rapid drug distribution within minutes in the early phase of delivery. Therefore, formulations should be designed to efficiently exploit the olfactory interface at the cribriform plate, which serves as a primary anatomical gateway for rapid CSF spread and anterior brain targeting (Figure 3) (Johnston et al. 2004; Nagra et al. 2006; Norwood and Zhang, 2019; Proulx 2021).

The trigeminal route initiates from the respiratory epithelium and forms a long transport axis along the peripheral nervous system toward the posterior CNS. Cargoes entering through the respiratory region reach compartments associated with terminal trigeminal fibers and migrate through the perineural, endoneurial, and epineurial spaces. They then progress along the larger trigeminal branches, including the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions, and the trigeminal ganglion, ultimately reaching the brainstem (Thorne et al. 2004; Lochhead and Davis 2019; Lochhead et al. 2019; Crowe and Hsu 2022). While cargoes that reach the brainstem may eventually redistribute into the SAS, this route functions to preferentially target the posterior and inferior regions of the CNS. Intranasally administered insulin, which localizes within the extracellular components and vessel-associated spaces of the trigeminal nerve layers, supports the existence of this peripheral-to-central transport axis (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Lochhead et al. 2019).

Ultimately, the olfactory route is ideal for anterior entry and rapid CSF-mediated spread, and the trigeminal route establishes a robust conduit to the posterior brainstem. Therefore, intranasal formulation must be strategically designed to target based on the spatial distribution of the intended neurological target (Thorne et al. 2004; Lochhead and Davis 2019; Lochhead et al. 2019; Crowe and Hsu 2022; Spera et al. 2023). As proof of concept, experimental models have shown that modifying the physicochemical properties of a therapeutic agent, such as altering its lipophilicity, molecular weight, or incorporating specific permeation enhancers, can actively shift its dominant transport trajectory between the olfactory-CSF and respiratory-trigeminal axes.

Even after successful entry through olfactory- or trigeminal-associated pathways, therapeutic cargoes rarely reach the brain parenchyma. Instead, a substantial fraction redistributes into CNS-associated fluid compartments. This stage is not a passive intermediate step but an independent bottleneck that constrains subsequent parenchymal penetration (Figure 4) (Iliff et al. 2012; Xie et al. 2013; Iliff et al. 2013; Proulx 2021; Spera et al. 2023).

The primary bottleneck at this stage is defined by compartmental partitioning. Post-entry transport does not follow a linear path. The administered cargo undergoes multilineage distribution, splitting among local tissues, meningeal surfaces, and circulating fluid channels (Johnston et al. 2004; Nagra et al. 2006; Lochhead et al. 2015; Lochhead and Davis 2019; Lochhead et al. 2019; Proulx 2021; Spera et al. 2023). For instance, while a fraction of the cargo entering via the olfactory route may achieve direct local tissue exposure, another fraction redistributes along the cribriform plate interface into the SAS or CSF. Consequently, only a limited fraction accesses the deeper parenchyma through perivascular spaces (PVS) and CSF-interstitial fluid (ISF) exchange (Iliff et al. 2012; Iliff et al. 2013; Mestre et al. 2018). Similarly, trigeminal-associated cargoes are repartitioned between brainstem tissue regions and adjacent fluid-associated compartments. The critical constraint of preferential enrichment in a fluid compartment does not guarantee tissue penetration. This creates a weak link between fluidic redistribution and parenchymal access, and the process is vulnerable to redistribution, secondary repartitioning, and diversion towards lymphatic drainage (Johnston et al. 2004; Nagra et al. 2006; Lochhead and Davis 2019; Lochhead et al. 2019; Proulx 2021).

The directionality of cargo movement is actively driven by CSF bulk flow, PVS structural continuity, and localized pressure gradients, with the coordinated beating of ependymal cilia serving as the primary biological engine (Iliff et al. 2012; Xie et al. 2013; Iliff et al. 2013; Lochhead et al. 2015; Faubel et al. 2016; Mestre et al. 2018). Therefore, these intricate hydrodynamic and anatomical conditions can be another significant hurdle in the redistribution process. Unfortunately, these dynamic fluid mechanics are frequently overlooked in current literature, creating a major interpretive blind spot. When a CSF- or surface-associated signal is observed, this oversight makes it unclear whether the signal reflects sustained, productive transport toward the tissue or merely a transient state prior to clearance. Ultimately, the conversion of fluid redistribution into target tissue access is context-dependent, dictated by active local exchange dynamics rather than simple physical continuity between compartments (Iliff et al. 2012; Xie et al. 2013; Iliff et al. 2013; Mestre et al. 2018).

Thus, broad dissemination across fluid pathways must not be translated into tissue access. As CSF, SAS, and PVS are fundamentally fluid-associated compartments rather than the parenchyma itself, signals detected at the brain surface, meninges, ventricles, or perivascular regions must be interpreted independently of true intraparenchymal distribution (Iliff et al. 2012; Iliff et al. 2013; Lochhead et al. 2015; Mestre et al. 2018; Lochhead and Davis 2019). Therefore, the evaluation of delivery success must move beyond the mere observation of CNS entry to rigorously determine whether initial fluidic redistribution is structurally and functionally coupled to target tissue penetration.

sections.title: Intraparenchymal extracellular diffusion: ECM and steric hindrance

paragraphs.en: The transition from fluidic exposure to deep tissue infiltration represents a formidable structural bottleneck in intranasal delivery. Accumulation in the CSF does not mean that a cargo will cross the fluid-tissue interface. The initial hurdle is the structural boundary separating fluid compartments from the parenchymal tissue. Cargoes that have reached the CSF or perivascular spaces (PVS) must cross formidable cellular and anatomical barriers, such as the pial surface, the glia limitans, or layers enriched in astrocytic endfeet, to reach the parenchyma (Iliff et al. 2012; Pizzo et al. 2018; Proulx 2021). These interfaces are selectively organized barriers composed of ECM and precise microarchitecture (Figure 5).

In vivo imaging and biodistribution studies utilizing large sizes of cargoes, such as monoclonal antibodies and viral vectors, frequently observe massive cargo accumulation trapped along the pial surface and within the PVS (Iliff et al. 2012; Pizzo et al. 2018). These findings show that the glia limitans and astrocytic endfeet form a size-exclusion filter, blocking large molecules from crossing out of fluid compartments. Consequently, the actual efficiency of parenchymal entry is strictly governed by the structural permeability of these boundaries, independent of the cargo concentration in the adjacent fluid. Even upon successfully crossing this interface, the brain parenchyma does not function as a free-diffusion space. High cell density, dense ECM, ISF flow, and electrostatic interactions impose strong physical limitations on cargo mobility. As a result, intraparenchymal spread is often highly restricted, confining the cargo to superficial layers or regions adjacent to entry points (Nance et al. 2012; Xie et al. 2013).

The in vivo diffusion studies utilizing multiple nanoparticle platforms have explicitly demonstrated that standard therapeutic carriers larger than the brain's ECM mesh size (typically ~100 nm), or those lacking dense surface passivation, are almost instantaneously immobilized by steric hindrance and adhesive forces, completely failing to penetrate deep tissue (Nance et al. 2012). Therefore, overcoming these extracellular matrix restrictions and avoiding steric trapping are mandatory biophysical prerequisites for achieving homogeneous therapeutic distribution throughout the targeted brain structures.

Crucially, deep intraparenchymal accumulation remains profoundly disconnected from cellular internalization (Zhuang et al. 2011; Alvarez-Erviti et al. 2011; Steinbach et al. 2016). While widespread tissue penetration is an absolute prerequisite, it is by no means a surrogate for productive target-cell engagement. The brain hosts diverse cell populations, including neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, each with distinct membrane properties and endocytic activities. Therefore, the cellular uptake efficiency of different cargoes can vary depending on the cell type. Cargoes will fail to exert a therapeutic effect if it only binds non-specifically to surfaces or are prematurely cleared by microglial phagocytosis (Zhuang et al. 2011). Thus, actual cellular internalization and functional engagement must be verified as a distinct, final hurdle separate from parenchymal penetration (Figure 6).

This multi-stage reality highlights the limitations of over-reliance on whole-brain homogenate data or bulk fluorescence to determine delivery success (Harmon et al. 2014; Lochhead et al. 2015; Ahmad et al. 2017; Lochhead and Davis 2019; Yokel 2022). Such ‘regional exposure’ metrics fail to distinguish whether a drug is merely trapped in perivascular or extracellular spaces, or it has entered intended target cells. Therefore, successful delivery requires strictly separating the evaluation of tissue accumulation from functional cellular engagement (Alvarez-Erviti et al. 2011; Harmon et al. 2014). The meaningful clinical translation of N2B delivery lies in providing clear mechanistic solutions for how a cargo will cross tissue boundaries, penetrate deeply into disease lesions, and ultimately engage with target cells (Lochhead and Davis 2019).

sections.title: Current formulation strategies to overcome stage-specific bottlenecks in N2B delivery
Physical interventions in the early nasal stage

paragraphs.en: Successful N2B delivery strategies should aim to maximize posterior nasal region, the gateway to effective brain delivery, rather than allowing formulations to mistarget the anterior impaction (Figure 7) (Kimbell et al. 2007; Foo et al. 2007; Djupesland 2013; Gao et al. 2020; Seifelnasr et al. 2024; Huang et al. 2024). The anterior nasal architecture, particularly the narrow ‘nasal valve,’ functions as a major aerodynamic filter that causes substantial dose loss to anterior impaction (Djupesland 2013). This limitation has been quantitatively validated by Kimbell et al., whose computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models showed that over 90% of standard 20–50 μm particles deposit anteriorly, though minor geometric or velocity adjustments can improve posterior access (Kimbell et al. 2007). Similarly, Foo et al. demonstrated using nasal replicas that narrowing the plume angle combined with a precise administration angle (shifting from 50° back to 30°) can dramatically boost turbinate deposition from ~15% to nearly 90%, highlighting the critical role of user positioning (Foo et al. 2007). To overcome these technique-dependent variances, Djupesland et al. introduced a breath-actuated bidirectional device that leverages the patient's exhaled air, this engineering approach successfully reduced anterior loss to ~14% and increased initial deposition in the critical superior–posterior region 3-fold from ~11% to ~32% (Djupesland et al. 2006). Collectively, these multi-level strategies have made anatomically targeted deposition the most mature engineering axis in N2B delivery.

Following anatomically targeted deposition, the second engineered axis focuses on local residence and mucus interaction (Gizurarson 1993; Merkus et al. 1998; Cone 2009; Boegh and Nielsen 2015). Even when deposition successfully occurs in anatomically favorable posterior regions, rapid MCC can wash away formulations within minutes, strictly restricting the opportunity for epithelial contact and subsequent transport. To actively circumvent this kinetic bottleneck, formulation engineering has shifted from simple solutions to advanced biomaterial platforms designed to prolong mucosal exposure.

As a primary and direct strategy to prevent early-stage drug loss, researchers have extensively developed in situ gelling systems, which undergo a sol-to-gel transition after administration (Mehta et al. 2009; Qian et al. 2014). In situ gelling systems combine the ease of liquid administration with instantaneous viscosity enhancement upon mucosal contact, effectively locking the formulation in place to resist MCC. Mehta et al. engineered a thermosensitive, poloxamer/HPMC-based in situ gel co-loaded with pheniramine and phenylephrine for sinusitis therapy (Mehta et al. 2009). In vivo gamma scintigraphy demonstrated that this formulation extended the nasal residence time to approximately 6 hours, effectively overcoming the rapid mucosal clearance that eliminated the standard drug solution within just 15 minutes. Similarly, Qian et al. utilized a poloxamer-based thermosensitive in situ gel, which represents an advanced platform that autonomously forms a stable gel using the physiological temperature of the nasal cavity without external chemical triggers (Qian et al. 2014). They reported that this system delayed mucociliary transport by more than 6-fold, ultimately increasing plasma and brain exposure by approximately 2- to 3-fold compared to conventional formulation. Collectively, these studies have established in situ gelling systems as one of the most direct and quantitatively validated physical interventions to extend nasal residence (Mehta et al. 2009; Qian et al. 2014).

To overcome the inherent kinetic limitations of such single-stimulus hydrogels, specifically the delayed gelation time of thermosensitive poloxamers, dual-responsive or multi-triggered in situ gelling systems have been developed (Chen et al. 2019; Agrawal et al., 2020; Gadhave et al. 2021). This strategy fused thermosensitive poloxamers with ion-responsive polysaccharides, such as gellan gum or sodium alginate. Upon intranasal administration, these hybrid platforms encounter simultaneous dual-stimuli. The temperature (37 °C) mediates thermal micellization of the poloxamer chains and endogenous cations (Ca+ and Na+) within the nasal mucus fluid trigger immediate ionic cross-linking of the polysaccharide domains. This multi-responsive axis is engineered to exhibit highly specialized shear-thinning rheological behavior. Under the high shear stress generated during spray actuation or administration, these polymer networks line up to lower viscosity, ensuring optimal atomization and targeted deposition. However, the moment the formulation contacts the mucosal interface and the shear rate drops to zero, the dual triggers prompt a sol-to-gel phase transition within a second. This abrupt viscosity escalation effectively anchors the formulation into a robust 3D matrix before the mechanical mucociliary sweeping action can initiate, thereby securely locking the therapeutic payload at the olfactory gateway.

Beyond simply modulating viscosity of cargo formulation, the engineering paradigm has advanced toward utilizing polymer-based mucoadhesive systems that actively resist MCC (Illum et al. 1994; Pritchard et al. 1996; Soane et al. 1999; Krauland et al. 2006). Chitosan and hyaluronic acid (HA) are the most representative mucoadhesive polymers due to their capacity for strong interfacial engagement with the hydrated mucus layer. Chitosan is a cationic polysaccharide containing protonatable primary amine groups that interact electrostatically with negatively charged sialic acid and sulfate residues in mucin glycoproteins (Aspden et al. 1997; Soane et al. 1999; Krauland et al. 2006). In the mucus environment, chitosan absorbs water and forms a gel-like interfacial layer, facilitating polymer-mucin interaction and prolonging nasal residence (Soane et al. 1999; Krauland et al. 2006). Importantly, conclusions regarding these natural polymers cannot be broadly generalized, as their physical behavior depends heavily on molecular weight and structural grades. For instance, lower-molecular-weight chitosan generally offers superior transmucosal permeation, whereas higher-molecular-weight variants provide stronger viscosity-driven mucoadhesion but weaker penetration (Chae et al. 2005; Bruinsmann et al. 2019). Therefore, explicitly reporting specific parameters, such as the exact molecular weight and degree of deacetylation for chitosan, or chain length for HA, is essential for reproducibility and meaningful cross-study comparisons. Aspden et al. directly evaluated this concept using ex vivo human nasal tissue treated with 0.25% chitosan salt solutions (Aspden et al. 1997). When nasally administered as a spray, chitosan transiently suppressed the mucociliary transport rate, reducing it to 0% of the baseline at 15 and 30 minutes before recovering by 90 to 120 minutes. This demonstrates that chitosan physically slows mucociliary transport.

Subsequently, chitosan was integrated into particulate formulation systems designed to retain cargo more effectively within the nasal cavity. Soane et al. extended this concept using chitosan polymer microspheres and compared the nasal clearance of different formulations in human volunteers (Soane et al. 1999). Specifically, chitosan microspheres significantly extended the nasal clearance half-life, achieving a 4- and 2-fold increase in retention time compared with a standard sodium fluorescein solution and unmodified chitosan solution, respectively (Soane et al. 1999). This study transitioned chitosan from a simple excipient to a polymer-based mucoadhesive platform, proving that particulate chitosan systems provide much stronger nasal residence.

Recent breakthroughs in N2B delivery highlight advanced hybrid platforms that structurally integrate the polycationic mucoadhesive functionality of chitosan with the robust protective capabilities of lipidic cores (Prego et al. 2006; Salade et al. 2017; Saini et al. 2021; Kapoor et al. 2025; Riani et al. 2026). Salade et al. developed an engineered nanoplatform for the N2B delivery of ghrelin by coating anionic liposomes with water-soluble quaternized chitosan (HTCC) (Salade et al. 2017). In this architecture, the internal liposomal core can electrostatically encapsulate and protect the peptide from nasal enzymatic degradation, while the external HTCC corona drives a significant increase in mucin adsorption capacity through enhanced electrostatic interactions. To validate these therapeutic advantages in vivo, Prego et al. evaluated chitosan-coated oily nanocapsules incorporating salmon calcitonin (sCT) as a model peptide (Prego et al. 2006). Following intranasal administration in rats, the sCT-loaded chitosan nanocapsules elicited a significantly more potent and prolonged hypocalcemic effect compared to both uncoated nanoemulsions and simple chitosan-containing aqueous solutions. Furthermore, Saini et al. demonstrated the preclinical relevance of this hybrid engineering paradigm specifically for Alzheimer's disease models. They generated ferulic acid-loaded solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) coated with chitosan via ionic gelation (Saini et al. 2021). The functionalized chitosan shell drastically enhanced ex vivo mucoadhesive strength on the nasal mucosa. Critically, the chitosan-coated SLNs demonstrated a 7-fold increase in brain ferulic acid concentrations relative to the pure drug, while achieving a significantly superior brain-to-plasma ratio compared to uncoated SLNs, underscoring the necessity of the hybrid core-shell architecture for achieving sustained therapeutic efficiency within the nasal cavity. These series of studies indicates that the structural coupling of lipidic core entrapment with a peripheral chitosan coating yields a potent synergistic intervention capable of efficiently overcoming kinetic clearance barriers at the nasal interface and accelerating brain drug targeting (Prego et al. 2006; Salade et al. 2017; Saini et al. 2021).

Nevertheless, native chitosan and its particulate formulations have intrinsic limitations regarding their restricted mucoadhesive persistence. Their mucoadhesion relies on reversible physical mechanisms that are vulnerable to continuous mucus turnover (Soane et al. 1999; Krauland et al. 2006). To this end, chitosan has been modified to overcome these limitations. For example, Krauland et al. utilized thiolated chitosan (Krauland et al. 2006). Mechanistically, thiolation introduces sulfhydryl groups into the chitosan backbone, enabling the formation of strong covalent disulfide bonds with mucin glycoproteins. This creates a robust matrix that provides swelling-driven retention and sustained drug release. The thiolated chitosan microparticles provided sustained release of a peptide cargo over approximately 6 hours and boosted absolute bioavailability by approximately 3.5-fold compared to unmodified native chitosan microparticles. This specific case proves that thiolation of chitosan is a derivative advancement that successfully extends the limited mucoadhesive persistence of native chitosan microparticles and maximizes peptide delivery performance.

Native hyaluronic acid (HA) is also highly valued for its exceptional water-retention capacity and viscoelasticity, which facilitate hydration, lubrication, and prolonged mucosal contact (Pritchard et al. 1996). Pritchard et al. directly evaluated this property using an excised frog palate model to assess the mucociliary transport delaying effect of hyaluronic acid (Pritchard et al. 1996). In this study, native hyaluronic acid completely inhibited transport, demonstrating a 100.0 ± 0.0% reduction rate, which validates that native hyaluronic acid functions as a potent mucociliary transport-delaying polymer. To advance these platforms further, chemically modified variants have been introduced. For instance, Laffleur et al. proposed a chemical modification introducing a cysteine group into the HA backbone (Laffleur et al. 2023). Cysteine modification enables thiol disulfide exchange interactions with the cysteine-rich domains of mucus glycoproteins, thereby establishing strong covalent bonds with the mucus. Cysteine-modified HA increased mucoadhesive potential by 3.26-fold, ex vivo tissue bioadhesion by 1.4-fold, and the nasal residence time of a model cargo by 1.74-fold relative to unmodified HA, shifting the platform from simple hydration to robust interfacial retention.

However, recent advancements suggest that simply maximizing mucoadhesion is not always the optimal solution (Cone 2009; Boegh and Nielsen 2015; Porfiryeva et al. 2021). Excessively strong adhesion can trap the cargo within the mucus network, paradoxically impeding its transport to the nasal epithelium. Ultimately, factors such as particle size, surface charge, and interfacial properties determine whether a cargo diffuses through or becomes immobilized, making the mucus layer a formidable physicochemical filter. Recognizing this limitation has driven a paradigm shift toward ‘mucus-penetrating’ systems, designed to preserve the cargo's transport capacity while minimizing unproductive mucus interactions. Porfiryeva et al. directly compared mucoadhesive interpolyelectrolyte nanoparticles with PEGylated controls (Porfiryeva et al. 2021). They found that the PEGylated nanoparticles bypassed adhesion and instead exhibited smooth mucus-penetrating behavior on sheep nasal mucosa, proving to be a highly viable alternative for in vivo N2B delivery. Direct mechanistic evidence for this mucus-stabilizing advantage was provided by Bazargani et al., who demonstrated using PEGylated solid lipid nanoparticles that increasing PEGylation effectively prevented mucin-mediated trapping by reducing the formation of large aggregates when incubated in artificial nasal mucus for 20 minutes at 37 °C (Bazargani et al. 2025). This structural stabilization directly translated to enhanced transport capability, allowing the 15 percent PEGylated formulation to dramatically increase apparent mucus permeability by 10.1 times without compromising cellular uptake in nasal epithelial cells.

Expanding upon this concept, native mucoadhesive polymers have been transformed into sophisticated mucus-penetrating platforms via strategic PEGylation (Ways et al. 2022; Gao et al. 2023). PEGylated chitosan-grafted amphiphilic micelles consist with chemically conjugating hydrophilic PEG chains and the cationic chitosan backbone. The highly localized positive surface charge of the primary amines is effectively masked at the outer particle interface. This steric and electrostatic shielding successfully prevents non-specific interactions with the negative domains of mucin glycoproteins, allowing the surface-tailored micelles to leverage their neutralized, highly hydrated corona to slip unimpeded through the mucosal meshwork. At the same time, the functional role of chitosan is repositioned within the nanostructure's interior. Beneath the protective PEG shell, the preserved primary amine groups of the chitosan backbone function as a potent electrostatic encapsulation core. This highly localized positive charge density drives spontaneous polyplex formation, aggressively packaging and protecting negatively charged biotherapeutic cargoes, such as therapeutic small interfering RNA (siRNA), messenger RNA (mRNA), or delicate peptide biologics, against aggressive nasal enzymatic degradation (Prego et al. 2006; Salade et al. 2017; Sava et al. 2020; Maniyamgama et al., 2025). Consequently, this hybrid architecture operates as a multifunctional vehicle. The outer PEG corona serves as a temporary stealth to bypass the mucociliary sweeping action, while the inner chitosan matrix acts as a robust, protective cage for fragile payloads, collectively ensuring highly efficient and structurally intact direct N2B transport.

The structural optimization of the mucus-penetrating strategies is not limited to polymeric backbones. Advanced lipid-based self-assembling systems have also emerged as a highly effective, physicochemical strategy to outmaneuver the mucosal barrier. As structurally stable colloidal systems typically prepared via high-pressure homogenization or microfluidics (Bonferoni et al. 2019; Bahadur et al. 2020), nanoemulsions offer a highly tunable platform that physicochemical properties dictate in vivo fate. Specifically, engineering the particle size below 200 nm significantly minimizes mucus entrapment and mucociliary clearance, thereby prolonging nasal residence time and maximizing epithelial uptake (Samaridou and Alonso 2018). Furthermore, tailoring the interfacial properties to achieve a zeta potential exceeding ±30 mV ensures robust colloidal stability, while introducing a positive surface charge facilitates strong electrostatic interaction with the negatively charged sialic acid residues of the nasal mucosa, effectively preventing premature dose loss (Chatterjee et al. 2019).

Importantly, this programmatic transition toward minimizing unproductive mucus interactions can be downscaled from particulate colloidal dispersions to the individual molecular level. Cyclodextrin-based platforms can also be conceptualized within this mucus-penetrating design axis (Rassu et al. 2015; Kali et al. 2024). Cyclodextrins act as amphiphilic penetration enhancers that utilize their lipophilic internal cavities to form inclusion complexes with drugs, thereby increasing aqueous solubility and preventing the cargo from being trapped in the mucin network to actively enhance mucus diffusion. Kali et al. comprehensively reviewed cyclodextrins and their derivatives as multifunctional delivery platforms, emphasizing that modified variants such as thiolated cyclodextrins can offer a diverse functional capability, including mucoadhesion, permeation enhancement, in situ gelation, and improved cellular uptake (Kali et al. 2024). Rassu et al. used methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) microparticles loaded with deferoxamine mesylate, a hydrophilic iron chelator drug (Rassu et al. 2015). The added methyl groups alter the hydrophobicity and steric environment around the cavity, enhancing complexation efficiency with drug molecules. In this study, MβCD microparticles showed approximately 1.6 times higher permeation capacity compared to deferoxamine alone and 13.6 times higher permeation capacity compared to the chitosan polymer. After intranasal administration in rats, MβCD microparticles demonstrated an approximately 3.8-fold higher drug concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid at 30 minutes post-administration compared to chitosan microparticles.

Taken together, these studies illustrate that local residence and mucus interaction constitute a critical early-stage bottleneck that the field has aggressively and extensively engineered. Through spray-angle modulation, in situ gelation, mucoadhesive polymer design, mucus-penetration engineering, and researchers have established a multifaceted framework of strategies to delay clearance, maximize epithelial exposure, and ultimately drive delivery efficiency (Table 2) (Djupesland et al. 2006; Krauland et al. 2006; Qian et al. 2014; Rassu et al. 2015; Bonferoni et al. 2019; Agrawal et al., 2020; Porfiryeva et al. 2021; Kali et al. 2024). Consequently, as with anatomically targeted deposition, this stage represents a highly mature, experimentally tractable intervention axis supported by a wealth of quantitative and mechanistic evidence.

sections.title: Biochemical and immunological constraints at the nasal interface

paragraphs.en: Beyond physical deposition and mucus interaction, intranasal delivery is also constrained by the biochemical and immunological environment of the nasal cavity (Figure 8) (Longo et al. 1986; Baron et al. 1988; Aceto et al. 1989; Gervasi et al. 1991; Sarkar 1992). Even when formulations are successfully deposited and retained locally, therapeutic cargoes may be exposed to enzymatic degradation, chemical destabilization, premature release, or immune-mediated inactivation before productive epithelial entry. This issue is particularly important for biologics, including peptides, proteins, nucleic acids, and viral vectors, whose structural integrity or biological activity can be rapidly compromised at the mucosal interface. Accordingly, biochemical instability and local immune exposure have become another actively targeted early-stage bottleneck in intranasal delivery.

One of the earliest and most direct demonstrations of this barrier came from studies of intranasally administered peptides. Hussain et al. showed that leucine enkephalin peptide underwent extensive hydrolysis within the rat nasal cavity at physiologically relevant concentrations (Hussain et al. 1985). Intact peptide rapidly declined and the extent of absorption was estimated to be less than ~10%. Notably, co-administered competing peptides successfully mitigated this hydrolysis and enhanced absorption. This protective ‘decoy’ effect proved that the primary barrier to delivery was not the impermeability of the nasal membrane itself. In this context, peptide absorption is strongly limited by rapid enzymatic degradation before epithelial crossing can occur.

Recognition of this barrier led to active investigation of protease inhibition strategies. O'Hagan et al. showed that coadministration of the aminopeptidase inhibitor amastatin significantly enhanced intranasal absorption of biosynthetic human growth hormone in rats, increasing peak plasma levels by 278% and relative bioavailability to approximately 28.9%, whereas bestatin showed little benefit (O'Hagan et al. 1990). Hussain et al. demonstrated that α-aminoboronic acid derivatives markedly stabilized leucine enkephalin in the nasal cavity (Hussain et al. 1989). In the presence of boroleucine, more than 90% of intact peptide remained after 45 minutes and approximately 85% remained after 90 minutes. Together, these studies established that improving intranasal delivery often requires preserving cargo integrity long enough for absorption (Hussain et al. 1989; O'Hagan et al. 1990).

This same principle becomes even more critical for nucleic acid therapeutics (Howard et al. 2006; Fihurka et al. 2018). In addition to nuclease-mediated degradation, nucleic acid cargoes are vulnerable to electrostatic interactions with mucus, aggregation or premature unpackaging under ionic conditions, and inefficient intracellular release after cellular uptake. To overcome these vulnerabilities, cationic polymers have emerged as a crucial strategy. Because siRNA is a strongly negatively charged hydrophilic macromolecule, utilizing cationic polymers is essential to condense nucleic acid therapeutics, such as siRNA, antisense oligonucleotide (ASO), and mRNA into nanoscale dimensions, mask their negative charge, and promote both mucus penetration and cellular uptake (Howard et al. 2006). Fihurka et al. directly demonstrated that nanoparticle packaging can shield nucleic acid cargoes from nuclease access (Fihurka et al. 2018). While naked DNA was completely degraded within 20 minutes of DNase I treatment, silica nanoparticles successfully preserved over 90% of the DNA at 20 minutes and approximately 70% at 60 minutes. Howard et al. demonstrated that the chitosan siRNA nanoparticles improve structural stability of siRNA under physiological conditions. Crucially, repeated intranasal administration of this platform in transgenic mice reduced EGFP-positive epithelial cells by 43%, demonstrating that the formulation retains sufficient biological activity after nasal delivery to induce robust mucosal gene silencing (Howard et al. 2006).

In contrast to shielding strategies that aim to preserve the intact carrier complex during mucosal transport, recent counterintuitive approaches have utilized the inherent biochemical properties of the nasal cavity to trigger interfacial dissociation, maximizing the penetration of the naked cargo (Zhang et al. 2023). In this novel strategy, the carrier acts merely as an ‘escort,’ safely transporting the cargo solely to the nasal wall and deliberately shedding it upon reacting to specific mucosal conditions. Zhang et al. developed a polymeric nanoDisc (polyDisc) system responsive to the slightly acidic microenvironment (pH ~6.5) of the nasal cavity for Alzheimer's disease treatment and showed that the carrier actively dissociated from the cargo at the mucosal interface. Specifically, they engineered a phenylboronic acid (PBA)-grafted chitosan polymer (CP) to package high-density lipoprotein discs (HDL-Disc). Their study demonstrated that the polyDisc actively depolymerized immediately upon reaching the mucosa, allowing the dissociated CP to exclusively act to open epithelial tight junctions while the carrier-free HDL-Disc slipped through the disrupted barrier to enter the brain. This design strategically subverts the biochemical constraints of the nasal cavity, utilizing the acidic environment not as a degradation threat but as a ‘penetration switch,’ thereby presenting a new paradigm in overcoming the initial nasal barrier by physically decoupling the roles of the carrier and cargo at the mucosal interface.

Local immune exposure represents a related but distinct early-stage constraint, particularly for biological and viral formulations that remain immunologically exposure state even when physically stabilized (Salzman et al. 1985; Quinn et al. 2011; Dey et al. 2016; El-Ayoubi et al. 2023; Zhao et al. 2025). In contrast to enzymatic degradation, which erodes cargo integrity directly, immune recognition can limit persistence, re-administration, and local tolerability. Quinn et al. showed that intranasally administered AAV12 effectively transduced the nasal epithelium while eliciting a lower immune response than AAV2, suggesting that a specific capsid variant can influence immune compatibility at the early stage of delivery (Quinn et al. 2011). Beyond serotype selection, delivery strategies have also been used to reduce extracellular immune exposure. Dey et al. used stem-cell-based shuttle systems to deliver oncolytic adenoviruses intranasally to glioblastoma, showing improved tumor-directed delivery after nasal administration (Dey et al. 2016). El-Ayoubi et al. likewise showed that optimized shuttle cells significantly improved intranasal delivery of oncolytic adenovirus to glioblastoma-bearing mice and extended survival (El-Ayoubi et al. 2023). In addition, polymer-coated viral systems such as the pH-sensitive polymeric oncolytic adenovirus reported by Zhao et al. may also reduce premature immune exposure before target-site activation (Zhao et al. 2025). Together, these findings show that early biochemical protection cannot be judged only by whether cargo survives. It must also be evaluated by whether the protective strategy reduces immunological visibility and extracellular loss without introducing a prohibitive local inflammatory burden at the nasal interface (Salzman et al. 1985; Quinn et al. 2011; Dey et al. 2016; El-Ayoubi et al. 2023; Zhao et al. 2025).

Viewed in this way, biochemical instability and local immune exposure occupy a distinct position from deposition or mucus residence. Whereas the earlier bottlenecks determine where and how long a formulation is present, this barrier determines whether the retained fraction remains biologically competent and immunologically tolerable. For this reason, the central challenge at this stage is not simply preservation in a generic sense, but preservation of a fraction that remains both transport-competent and locally acceptable (Table 3).

sections.title: Epithelial crossing through modulating paracellular and transcellular entry

paragraphs.en: As outlined in Section 2.2, the epithelial crossing stage represents a critical branching point where several transport mechanisms, mostly the paracellular route (going between cells) and the transcellular route (going through cells), can either compete or cooperate (Figure 9). The specific route can dictate the downstream trajectory of cargo within the CNS (Lin et al. 2016; Lochhead and Davis 2019; Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025; Qiu et al. 2025).

Faced with these competing pathways, researchers sought to target the paracellular route as the first line of approach, modulating apical junctional complexes to transiently increase paracellular permeability (Aungst 2012). This is supported by Min et al. who demonstrated that local hypoxic stimuli can significantly reduce transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and downregulate key junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and E-cadherin (Min et al. 2015). To this end, chitosan-based formulations have been engineered as an epithelial permeation enhancer. For instance, Zhang et al. showed that 0.5% chitosan markedly enhanced the in vitro permeability coefficient of FITC-labeled recombinant hirudin-2, a thrombin-inhibiting anticoagulant peptide, across excised nasal epithelium and increased its in vivo nasal bioavailability up to 8.26% compared to saline controls (Zhang et al. 2005). Moreover, combining chitosan with surfactants like SDS or Tween 80 further increased the nasal bioavailability of recombinant hirudin-2 up to 17.25%, while maintaining acceptable ciliotoxicity.

These early studies established that the epithelial layer should not be considered as a fixed boundary, but rather as dynamic gateway which is capable of modulation. This strategy has subsequently been refined using pH-resilient chitosan derivatives, ensuring functional efficacy across varied physiological conditions (du Plessis et al. 2010). Because unmodified chitosan retains its protonated and soluble state only under acidic conditions, its junction-opening capability is lost as the pH shifts toward neutral. To overcome this limitation, du Plessis et al. compared chitosan hydrochloride with highly quaternized N-trimethyl chitosan chloride (TMC) for intranasal insulin delivery. While all polymers enhanced insulin absorption at pH 4.40, only the highly quaternized TMC sustained its enhancing effect at pH 7.40, resulting in about 5-fold increase in insulin levels. This indicated that epithelial permeation is dependent on its ability to preserve ionization within the shifting physicochemical environment of the nasal cavity.

Beyond polymeric matrices, cyclodextrin-based platforms have emerged as chemical permeation enhancers that modulate epithelial membrane lipids and tight-junction organization (Marttin et al., 1999; Merkus et al., 1999; Yang et al. 2004). Cyclodextrins form complexes with membrane lipids which temporarily loosen the dense network of epithelial tight junctions and modulate localized epithelial membrane fluidity. Marttin et al. provided direct morphological evidence for structural changes in tight junctions using electron and confocal microscopy in the rat nasal respiratory epithelium following the application of methyl β-cyclodextrin (Marttin et al., 1999). Supporting these physical changes, Yang et al. reported that 5% dimethyl β-cyclodextrin induced the redistribution of the tight junction marker ZO-1 and decreased epithelial integrity to actively promote paracellular pathway opening (Yang et al. 2004). Crucially, this permeation-enhancing effect was fully reversible within 6 hours in vivo and effectively increased the absolute bioavailability of intranasal enoxaparin by approximately eight times. Based on these mechanisms, Merkus et al. demonstrated that dimethyl β-cyclodextrin significantly promoted the nasal absorption of insulin or ACTH analogs compared to liquid controls, achieving 70 to 100% bioavailability in mouse models (Merkus et al., 1999).

The concept of barrier penetration has been expanded from intercellular gap opening in epithelial cells to enzymatic strategies that directly target the extracellular matrix structurally supporting them (Lochhead et al. 2015; Yokel 2022). Lochhead et al. demonstrated that matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), which degrades tight junctions and extracellular matrix components, significantly increased the permeability of 10 kDa dextran across the olfactory epithelium, illustrating that modulating structural nasal epithelial permeability can actively enhance particle delivery (Lochhead et al. 2015). In a similar context, hyaluronidase has been also explored to increase tissue permeability (Danielyan et al. 2009; Galeano et al. 2018). The hyaluronidase pretreatment successfully facilitated nasal cellular uptake and maximized stem cell trafficking to the brain. However, there is a clear limitation in interpreting this as direct evidence of improved nasal epithelial permeability. It remains unclear whether the increased absorption is precisely due to enhanced penetration across the epithelial cell layer itself or the degradation of other tissue matrices located beyond the epithelium. Furthermore, whether these macroscopic matrix-modifying pretreatments can directly enhance the absorption of synthetic nanomedicines or conventional small molecules has not yet been clearly reported. Consequently, verifying biological mechanisms for nanocarrier systems remains a critical objective requiring rigorous validation (Danielyan et al. 2009; Galeano et al. 2018; Yokel 2022).

Another major strategy focused on utilizing transcellular uptake mechanisms (Malhotra et al., 2013; Lin et al. 2016). This approach is particularly critical for macrobiologics such as siRNA, mRNA, and plasmid DNA, which are intrinsically restricted from passive paracellular diffusion due to their large molecular weight and negative charge density (Howard et al. 2006; Malhotra et al., 2013; Lin et al. 2016). To overcome this limitation, cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs), which are cationic or amphipathic short amino acid sequences, are utilized to cross the epithelial cell membrane (Malhotra et al., 2013; Lin et al. 2016). Despite strategies targeting the transcellular route are increasing, most studies only demonstrate cellular uptake or brain distribution without directly proving epithelial transcytosis (Malhotra et al., 2013; Schlachet and Sosnik 2019; Yokel 2022). To claim transcytosis, it requires evidence such as apical internalization, intracellular vesicular trafficking, basolateral release, paracellular exclusion, and pathway inhibition. For example, Malhotra et al. engineered PEGylated chitosan nanoparticles, which were functionalized with dual MGF and TAT peptide tags, a representative CPPs, for siRNA delivery (Malhotra et al., 2013). In this system, chitosan provided mucoadhesive matrix, PEGylation offered steric stabilization, and the TAT and MGF peptide tags were integrated for membrane interaction and transcellular uptake. Although this system showed robust siRNA localization in the cerebral cortex and cerebellum within 4 hours of post-administration without inducing detectable neurotoxicity, it is a proof of concept for peptide-mediated brain delivery rather than direct proof of epithelial transcytosis. The underlying evaluation lacked the mechanistic resolution to differentiate transcellular crossing from paracellular, nerve-associated, or systemic pathways.

Ligand mediated uptake strategies present a similar methodological limitation (Schlachet and Sosnik 2019; Yokel 2022). Gabold et al. evaluated transferrin-decorated chitosan nanoparticles for nose-to-brain delivery of β-galactosidase as a model protein cargo (Gabold et al. 2023). In this study, transferrin was decorated on the surface of chitosan nanoparticles (CNs) after particle formation through copper-free click chemistry. This strategy minimizes undesired cargo-ligand interactions and allows modulation of surface ligands while preserving the protein cargo inside the nanoparticle. In an air–liquid interface (ALI) nasal epithelial model, encapsulation in chitosan nanoparticles increased cellular uptake of β-galactosidase, and transferrin decoration further enhanced uptake compared with non-decorated nanoparticles and free protein. However, such enhanced intracellular localization should not be equated with successful epithelial crossing. Confirming true receptor-mediated transcytosis requires rigorous tracking of the apical-to-basolateral transport of the intact cargo, definitive basolateral release, and the preservation of barrier integrity under competitive receptor-blocking conditions (Schlachet and Sosnik 2019; Yokel 2022).

Even when cellular internalization is successfully achieved, it is not automatically translated into epithelial crossing, these nucleic acid cargoes remain highly vulnerable to endosomal sequestration and premature intracellular degradation (Howard et al. 2006; Malhotra et al., 2013; Harmon et al. 2014). To circumvent post-uptake endosomal sequestration, Harmon et al. applied CK30PEG-compacted plasmid DNA nanoparticles, utilizing a 30-mer poly-lysine peptide to package large nucleotide structures into a protective PEGylated shell (Harmon et al. 2014). Following intranasal administration, widespread eGFP expressions were observed along the rostral-caudal axis of the rat brain. By providing transgene expression as the delivery outcome, this study confirms that CK30PEG can preserve the cargo's structural integrity throughout the entire transport. This represents a critical frame evolution from strictly focused on maximizing initial epithelial uptake to designing carriers capable of sustaining cargo biological function throughout the post-entry stages.

In summary, the nasal epithelium has been aggressively engineered through tight-junction modulation, pH-resilient paracellular enhancers, CPP-assisted uptake, and endosomal-escape machinery (Marttin et al., 1999; Merkus et al., 1999; Yang et al. 2004; Zhang et al. 2005; Danielyan et al. 2009; du Plessis et al. 2010; Aungst 2012; Malhotra et al., 2013; Min et al. 2015; Galeano et al. 2018; Schlachet and Sosnik 2019; Gabold et al. 2023). Despite these technological milestones, most literature concludes epithelial crossing success indirectly from downstream brain signals or reporter gene expression (Malhotra et al., 2013; Harmon et al. 2014; Schlachet and Sosnik 2019; Yokel 2022; Gabold et al. 2023). There are limited studies directly quantifying the exact fraction of cargo that traverses the epithelium in a transport-competent state. Although epithelial crossings are still one of the most intensively targeted parts of N2B formulation, paradoxically, they still require mechanical and biological validation (Table 4).

sections.title: Post-epithelial gateways by navigating anatomical and fluidic pathways

paragraphs.en: This indicates that the immediate post-epithelial transport stage remains a critical gap and a completely uncharted territory in the design of drug delivery systems (Figure 10) (Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025). The mechanisms such as perineural transport along the olfactory and trigeminal nerves, CSF-mediated redistribution, and deep penetration into the brain parenchyma have received little attention in intranasal formulation design (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025). Although perineural transport into the brain is a well-established primary biological pathway following intranasal administration, there is a blank of formulation engineering that controls delivery efficiency by directly targeting the microfluidic or anatomical characteristics of these perineural spaces (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Lochhead et al. 2019; Spera et al. 2023). Indeed, several studies have highlighted the lack of evidence that nanosystems reach the brain parenchyma intact (Costa et al. 2019; Yokel 2020). While chitosan has been shown to enhance absorption from the nasal cavity into the brain or CSF, research demonstrating the intact translocation of nanoparticles deep into the brain parenchyma remains rare (Casettari and Illum 2014).

To overcome these barriers, pharmacological pretreatment strategies that modulate CSF dynamics and external physical-force-based approaches have been explored (Shingaki et al. 2009; Shingaki et al. 2010; Chen et al. 2014; Ye et al. 2021; Ye et al. 2023; Koh et al. 2026). In an intriguing example of chemical modulation, Shingaki et al. demonstrated that decreasing CSF production by acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, significantly increased the CSF concentrations of intranasally administered 5-fluorouracil and methotrexate. This approach offers a promising option for targeted drug delivery by inhibiting CSF production to reduce drug clearance. Additionally, approaches that physically overcome fluidic resistance using external electromagnetic forces or ultrasound are being explored. Ye et al. first demonstrated that transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-generated pulsed magnetic fields, applied concurrently with intranasal administration of magnetic nanoparticles, can actively drive particles across the cribriform plate and into the brain parenchyma, achieving approximately two-fold greater brain delivery compared to passive intranasal administration alone (Ye et al. 2023). Building on this proof of concept, Koh et al. subsequently conjugated temozolomide to superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (TMZ-SPIONs) and guided them intranasally to an intracranial glioblastoma site using TMS, demonstrating that magnetically directed N2B delivery significantly prolonged survival in xenograft mouse models while requiring less than one-tenth of the conventional drug dose (Koh et al. 2026). Separately, focused ultrasounds have been employed to augment intranasal delivery through distinct mechanisms. The active propulsion of anti-PD-L1 antibodies into the brainstem via ultrasound-enhanced delivery, or the hemisphere-specific enhancement of DNA nanoparticle gene expression through ultrasound pretreatment, suggests that physical energy can potently facilitate parenchymal penetration (Chen et al. 2014; Ye et al. 2021). However, these approaches remain supplementary strategies that overcome hydrodynamic resistance through dependence on external devices, and their clinical scalability is constrained by the need for specialized equipment and precise spatial targeting (Chen et al. 2014; Ye et al. 2021; Ye et al. 2023; Koh et al. 2026).

The strategy for achieving brain parenchymal penetration through the formulation's integral physicochemical properties, without external devices, involves biomimetic systems based on high-density lipoprotein (HDL) or apoA-I nanodiscs (Zhang et al. 2023). Designed to be ultrasmall, these nanodiscs biologically mimic the endogenous lipid transport pathways that are naturally present within the brain. This characteristic prevents non-specific entanglement from steric hindrances of the densely interwoven extracellular matrix (ECM), enabling them to penetrate deep into brain tissue. The N2B delivery of ASO-loaded apoA-I nanodiscs resulted in neuron-specific accumulation along the anterior–posterior axis (Aly et al. 2023). While ASO alone reached the perivascular space but failed to breach the matrix barrier, the nanodisc formulation capitalized on its superior matrix permeability to significantly reduce target gene expression in the cortex and striatum, thereby proving functional neural delivery. Furthermore, Zhang et al. engineered HDL discs to actively release under the mildly acidic conditions of the nasal cavity, capture amyloid-β within the brain parenchyma, and induce clearance mechanisms (Zhang et al. 2023). This approach drastically reduced amyloid-β accumulation in the brain parenchyma by up to 97.3% following administration.

Ultimately, the post-epithelial gateway, which governs the behavior of the cargo following epithelial transit, is the defining point of effective drug delivery. It dictates the precise compartmental distribution of the cargo and its capacity to penetrate the brain parenchyma (Nance et al. 2012; Pizzo et al. 2018; Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025). However, strategies driven purely by intranasal formulation engineering remain severely lacking compared with the research advancements seen in other routes of administration (Costa et al. 2019; Yokel 2020; Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025). Therefore, this is the key area that must be addressed as a priority in future formulation development (Table 5).

After reaching the brain parenchyma, the final goal in N2B delivery is precise engagement at the target site that aligns with the cargo's therapeutic mechanism (Figure 11) (Zhuang et al. 2011; Alvarez-Erviti et al. 2011; Harmon et al. 2014; Steinbach et al. 2016). The definition of successful delivery must vary depending on the characteristics of the cargo. Further, many cargoes, such as small molecules, peptides, siRNA, ASOs, plasmid DNA, and viral vectors, must enter disease-relevant cells to exert their functional activity, whereas other therapeutics act on extracellular targets and therefore do not require cellular internalization.

The most representative approach is receptor-mediated uptake which actively internalizes the cargo into cells by introducing specific ligands onto the carrier surface (Gabold et al. 2023). It targets receptors overexpressed on the surface of specific diseased cells or brain-related cells. Ferritin is an endogenous protein complex that stores iron in the body (Fan et al. 2012; Moglia et al. 2021). It forms a natural nanoscale cage structure, making it highly suitable for loading therapeutic drugs. Fan et al. and Moglia et al. demonstrated that H-ferritin nanocages target TfR1-rich brain tumor cells without any artificial chemical modifications. This intrinsically receptor-recognizing nanocage improves drug delivery to brain tumor cells, increasing cellular uptake by more than 7-fold. Furthermore, when applied to glioma therapy, this approach increased the cargo concentration in the tumor-bearing hemisphere by 5-fold and reduced tumor volume by up to 74% following intranasal administration (Marrocco et al. 2024).

Another major pathway to target is the lactoferrin (Lf)-lactoferrin receptor (LfR) axis. LfRs are abundantly expressed on the surface of major CNS-related cells, including brain vascular endothelial cells (Hu et al. 2009; Bi et al. 2016; Zhao et al. 2018). Thus, Lf-decorated carriers may facilitate receptor-associated entry into brain tissue and neural cells. Hu et al. demonstrated that Lf-conjugated PEG-PLA nanoparticles induced receptor-associated uptake in mouse brain microvascular endothelial cells and showed a 3-fold improvement in brain delivery efficiency in vivo compared with non-targeted PEG-PLA nanoparticles (Hu et al. 2009). Zhao et al. developed an Lf-modified nanostructured lipid carrier (Lf-NLC) loaded with nimodipine, a poorly water-soluble calcium-channel blocker, and showed enhanced receptor-mediated uptake and brain-targeting performance (Zhao et al. 2018).

Building on the same receptor-ligand logic, recent work has begun to extend N2B targeting from broad brain accumulation toward defined anatomical regions and individual cell types, although this remains an emerging capability. At the regional level, Rao et al. constructed hypothalamus-directed nanoparticles bearing a modified (Trp7, β-Ala8)-neurokinin A (4–10) ligand against the hypothalamic neurokinin three receptor (NK3R), which drove preferential uptake into hypothalamic cells after intranasal administration (Rao et al. 2024). Route-dependent bias offers a complementary handle, as olfactory transport favors rostral structures whereas trigeminal input preferentially reaches caudal regions such as the brainstem, so that ligand choice and administration route can jointly shape regional distribution (Lochhead and Davis 2019; Crowe and Hsu 2022; Spera et al. 2023). At the cellular level, surface ligands can steer carriers toward particular glial populations. Transferrin and lactoferrin decoration has been used to bias uptake toward astrocytes and tumor-associated glia, and intranasal platforms that reprogram microglia through lactoferrin-functionalized carriers or exploit the microglial tropism of exosomes have been demonstrated in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative models (Zhuang et al. 2011; Dlamini et al. 2026). These examples indicate that region- and cell-type-selective N2B delivery is feasible in principle, yet current selectivity derives largely from receptor abundance and anatomical routing rather than from absolute molecular specificity, leaving precise single-target engagement an open challenge.

Receptor-independent, cell-penetrating peptide (CPP)-mediated membrane engagement strategies are also widely utilized (Malhotra et al., 2013; Lin et al. 2016; Steinbach et al. 2016; Khafagy et al. 2020). CPPs are short amino acid sequences with strong positive charges or amphiphilicity. CPPs interact electrostatically with the negatively charged components of the cell membrane surface, temporarily loosening the membrane structure or inducing active endocytosis (Lin et al. 2016; Steinbach et al. 2016; Khafagy et al. 2020). Steinbach et al. demonstrated that when various CPPs such as penetratin, EB1, and MPG were introduced into PLGA nanoparticles, the energy-dependent and clathrin-mediated cell internalization of the nanoparticles improved by 48- to 64-fold compared to unmodified NPs (Steinbach et al. 2016). Lin et al. utilized LMWP, an arginine-rich CPP, to promote the brain entry of protein cargoes. Using horseradish peroxidase (HRP) and β-galactosidase (β-gal) as functional enzyme cargoes, they further showed that LMWP-linked enzymes retained measurable enzymatic activity in brain tissue, with significantly higher activity than their native, non-modified counterparts (Lin et al. 2016). Furthermore, Khafagy et al. co-administered leptin with penetratin, a type of CPP, and demonstrated not only brain accumulation but also CNS pharmacodynamic signaling, including STAT3 phosphorylation and leptin receptor stimulation (Khafagy et al. 2020).

Another strategy uses the native tropism of exosomes or cells (Zhuang et al. 2011; Dey et al. 2016; El-Ayoubi et al. 2023). Zhuang et al. intranasally administered exosome-encapsulated curcumin and observed exosome-positive signals in a substantial fraction of microglia, the target brain cells, within 1 hour (Zhuang et al. 2011). Further, it delayed brain inflammation and tumor growth. Dey et al. and El Ayoubi et al. intranasally administered an oncolytic adenovirus using a stem cell with migration characteristics toward the glioma microenvironment (Dey et al. 2016; El-Ayoubi et al. 2023). This approach is a unique strategy that extends survival not through target cell endocytosis, but by guiding the therapeutic viral cargo to the lesion via the tumor-homing behavior of a living carrier.

There are also conditional activation strategies that regulate cargo release or receptor accessibility in response to the lesion or disease microenvironment (Marrocco et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2025). The-0504 is a carrier designed to activate exclusively within the target tissue (Marrocco et al. 2024). The PASE shielding domain is a protective polypeptide module that masks the TfR1-binding surface of H-ferritin (HFt) and suppresses premature receptor binding until it is removed by MMP-2/9-mediated linker cleavage in the glioma microenvironment. Consequently, the exposed HFt is internalized by TfR1-overexpressing tumor cells, where it releases its payload (Genz-644282) to inhibit topoisomerase I. Ultimately, this single formulation can induce tumor receptor targeting and protease-responsive activation. In addition, protease-responsive linkers can be designed to remove shielding groups or release payloads using lesion-associated enzymes such as MMP-2/9, cathepsins, and legumain.

Tumor microenvironments of glioma often exhibit lower pH, higher ROS, and higher protease activity than normal tissues (Marrocco et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2025). Therefore, pH-responsive systems can induce carrier disassembly and cargo release in an acidic tumor microenvironment or endosomal pH. For instance, the polyDisc system developed by Zhang et al. exploits the mildly acidic nasal and endosomal pH to trigger carrier depolymerization, enabling selective cargo release at the target interface (Zhang et al. 2023). Similarly, protease-responsive platforms exploit lesion-associated enzymes such as MMP-2/9 to trigger shielding removal and selective cargo activation, as exemplified by the ferritin-based The-0504 nanovector described above (Marrocco et al. 2024). Further, ROS-responsive linkers can accelerate drug release in lesion areas with high oxidative stress. Zhang et al. demonstrated this principle by engineering thioketal-crosslinked nanoparticles loaded with puerarin, a neuroprotective natural flavonoid, and decorated with a mitochondria-targeting peptide (SS-31) (Zhang et al. 2023). These nanoparticles were intranasally administered via the nose-to-brain pathway in a middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) rat model of ischemic stroke. The thioketal linker enabled H₂O₂-dependent drug release, with cumulative release reaching approximately 48% under oxidative conditions compared to only 18% at baseline. In MCAO rat models, this approach reduced infarct volume approximately 3-fold compared to untreated controls, while alleviating oxidative stress and restoring mitochondrial function. These strategies can be applied not only in tumor targeting but also in CNS diseases where the lesion microenvironment is altered, such as neuroinflammation, ischemic injury, and neurodegenerative lesions (Zhuang et al. 2011; Marrocco et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2025). Even though stimuli-responsive platforms, such as protease-sensitive ferritin-based nanovectors and pH- or photo-responsive polymeric viral systems, have been actively explored, their application remains largely confined to the experimental proof-of-concept stage in CNS tumor therapy (Marrocco et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2025).

On the other hand, direct binding or clearance of extracellular misfolded protein aggregates or neurotoxic assemblies can establish sufficient therapeutic outcomes without requiring cellular uptake (Zhang et al. 2023; Li et al. 2025).
