The HDL-Disc-based polyDisc system developed by Zhang et al. functions not only as a carrier but also as a therapeutic unit that captures amyloid-β (Zhang et al. 2023). It can induce clearance mechanisms in the central and peripheral nervous systems, achieving a 97.3% reduction in brain parenchymal and a 73.5% reduction in vascular amyloid-β accumulation following intranasal administration. This logic extends to antibody-based agents that engage soluble or aggregated species in the interstitial space. Kamei et al. intranasally co-administered an anti-amyloid-β antibody with L-penetratin, achieving more efficient brain delivery than intravenous injection and improving spatial learning in aged App knock-in mice, while the increased soluble amyloid-β pool was consistent with suppressed plaque formation and microglia-associated clearance (Kamei et al. 2022).

Full-length antibodies carry an Fc effector domain that can provoke inflammatory or microhemorrhagic responses, motivating the exploration of antibody fragments. Cattepoel et al. showed that an anti-amyloid-β single-chain variable fragment (under 30 kDa) entered the cortex and hippocampus after chronic intranasal treatment, bound directly to parenchymal and vascular plaques, and reduced plaque burden and cerebral amyloid angiopathy without the Fc-mediated liabilities of the parent immunoglobulin (Cattepoel et al. 2011). Beyond binding-based sequestration, catalytic peptides can degrade aggregates enzymatically. Hatakawa et al. reported that JAL-TA9, a nine-residue catalytide hydrolyzing amyloid-β42, reached the cerebrospinal fluid at a concentration 4.8-fold higher than in plasma after intranasal administration, with direct transport percentages above 90% across the olfactory bulb, frontal, and occipital regions (Hatakawa et al. 2025). These strategies share a defining feature: the endpoint is engagement with an extracellular substrate rather than intracellular delivery (Table 6).

sections.title: Biofate and clearance of N2B delivery systems

paragraphs.en: The preceding strategies address how a delivery system overcomes each sequential bottleneck, yet its ultimate fate within the brain is governed by the biomolecular identity it acquires in transit rather than by its as-synthesized properties alone. Surface charge and charge density are the primary determinants of this acquired identity (Illum et al. 1994; Pritchard et al. 1996; Soane et al. 1999; Krauland et al. 2006). In the nasal cavity, highly cationic lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) adsorb negatively charged mucins to form an adhesive corona that, while prolonging residence, can entrap the carrier and consign it to mucociliary clearance before epithelial transit (Aspden et al. 1997; Soane et al. 1999). Consistent with this, a systematic screen of ionizable lipid nanoparticles showed that a positive surface charge enhances nose-to-brain delivery by prolonging nasal residence and driving brain-specific mRNA expression, underscoring surface charge as a tunable determinant of N2B efficiency (Yu et al. 2026). Once the carrier reaches the perineural spaces or CSF, this layer evolves as mucosal proteins are exchanged for endogenous components such as apolipoproteins and albumin. The identity of the acquired proteins can steer subsequent handling. In plasma and blood–brain barrier models, apolipoprotein E (ApoE) adsorption promotes recognition by low-density lipoprotein receptors (LDLRs), and an analogous route may operate in the N2B context, whereas enrichment with opsonins instead favors phagocytic removal by macrophages and, in the CNS, microglia (Wagner et al. 2012; Vu et al. 2019). The corona therefore acts less as a fixed design feature than as a determinant of where, and how rapidly, a carrier is ultimately cleared.

Understanding how these systems exit the brain is as important as understanding their entry. Clearance proceeds through several parallel routes that extend beyond the enzymatic hydrolysis of peptides, proteins, and oligonucleotides. Convective exchange along the glymphatic system moves solutes between the CSF and the interstitial fluid, after which macromolecules and intact carriers drain from the CNS largely through meningeal lymphatic vessels and perineural routes crossing the cribriform plate toward the cervical lymph nodes (Chae et al. 2024). Notably, this outflow is anatomically concentrated. A discrete arachnoid region surrounding the olfactory bulbs was recently shown to contain abundant fenestrations that serve as principal exit portals for CSF into the olfactory meningeal lymphatics, a pathway conserved in non-human primates and markedly diminished with aging (Hong et al. 2026). For low-molecular-weight species released from a carrier, efflux transporters at the blood‒brain barrier, most notably P-glycoprotein, actively pump substrates from the parenchyma back into the blood, a route that acts on the freed payload rather than on the intact nanocarrier (Cox et al. 2023). The nanocarriers themselves are instead handled predominantly by glial phagocytosis and perivascular drainage. These convective, lymphatic, cellular, and transporter-mediated pathways collectively set the residence time of a delivery system, which in turn defines both its therapeutic window and its potential for unintended accumulation.

This balance between residence and removal carries direct safety and toxicological implications central to regulatory evaluation (Keller et al. 2022). Given that the N2B route deposits material along the olfactory and trigeminal pathways and that repeated dosing is often required for chronic CNS conditions, impaired or saturated clearance raises the prospect of progressive nanomaterial accumulation in the olfactory bulb and perivascular compartments, sustained microglial activation, and local injury to the nasal epithelium. Conversely, because the same lymphatic outflow that clears waste can also remove a therapeutic before it acts, delivery and clearance must be considered as coupled design constraints rather than in isolation. Regulatory agencies accordingly expect biofate and safety profiles to be comprehensively evaluated alongside therapeutic efficacy. This includes not only biodistribution and systemic persistence, but also potential immunogenicity (both innate mucosal responses and systemic neutralizing immunity), neuroinflammation markers (astrogliosis and chronic microglial activation), and the overall reversibility of localized tissue effects.

sections.title: Future perspectives: overcoming the translational barriers in N2B delivery

paragraphs.en: The clinical landscape of intranasal CNS therapy reveals a pronounced translational imbalance. Agents that have reached regulatory approval are almost exclusively low-molecular-weight small molecules delivered as nasal sprays, including esketamine for treatment-resistant depression (Daly et al. 2018), zavegepant for acute migraine (Lipton et al. 2023), and midazolam and diazepam for seizure clusters (Detyniecki et al. 2019; Wheless et al. 2021). Peptide-based candidates, such as intranasal insulin for Alzheimer's disease, remain confined to early clinical testing (Craft et al. 2020). In contrast, the nanoplatform-based systems that dominate preclinical innovation, spanning chitosan nanoparticles, lipid nanoparticles, ferritin nanocages, and biomimetic nanodiscs, have yet to advance beyond rodent models (Zhang et al. 2023; Aly et al. 2023; Marrocco et al. 2024). This disparity indicates that formulation sophistication alone has not translated into clinical progress, pointing to unresolved barriers in the transport cascade rather than in cargo design. Successful N2B delivery strategies should aim to maximize posterior access, the gateway to effective brain delivery, rather than allowing formulations to mistarget the anterior region (Yokel 2022; Crowe and Hsu 2022; Drath et al. 2025). A fundamental engineering oversight driving this translational gap is the scarcity of formulation strategies that actively target post-epithelial fluidic and tissue-access pathways (Yokel 2020; Yokel 2022). These pathways range from the immediate post-epithelial transit to just prior to target cell internalization. Current formulation strategies have disproportionately optimized only the initial and final stages of delivery, focusing heavily on mucosal retention and epithelial permeation alongside ligand-directed target-cell engagement (Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025). Concurrently, they have largely neglected the intermediate post-epithelial channels, namely CSF/perivascular space (PVS)-mediated redistribution and deep parenchymal penetration (Yokel 2020; Yokel 2022). As a result, the lack of strategies to navigate these intermediate biological bottlenecks can render even sophisticated targeting ligands ineffective, relegating otherwise promising technologies to mere conceptual possibilities. Therefore, bridging this translational gap requires a paradigm shift toward multistage-aware formulation design capable of orchestrating the entire transport cascade.

Because N2B transport is a sequence of interconnected stages, maximizing the efficiency of a single stage can inadvertently introduce physicochemical trade-offs that compromise subsequent transport phases (Lai et al. 2009; Suk et al. 2016; Yokel 2022). A representative example is robust mucoadhesion. While it effectively extends nasal residential time, it simultaneously occupies therapeutic cargoes within the dense mucus mesh, thereby hindering their diffusion toward the epithelial surface (Cone 2009; Lai et al. 2009). Conversely, PEGylation designed to facilitate mucus penetration often compromises subsequent cellular uptake efficiencies (Suk et al. 2016). Furthermore, the surface conjugation of targeting ligands frequently impairs the mucus-penetrating properties of the formulation (Lai et al. 2009; Suk et al. 2016). These contradictory requirements across sequential barriers highlight why a multistage-aware design that systematically harmonizes the entire transport cascade is a key mechanistic requirement.

Recent formulation design has evolved beyond single-function maximization toward the spatiotemporal integration of complementary functionalities. The primary stage of this progress focused on a simple bidirectional integration, typically combining a cationic mucoadhesive backbone with a brain-targeting ligand within a single platform to simultaneously enhance nasal retention and receptor-mediated transcytosis (Meng et al. 2018). It has recently advanced into multi-layered sequential cascades designed to orchestrate triple-targeting properties, encompassing the mucus barrier, the epithelial cell layer, and specific intracellular uptake (Rassu et al. 2017). A single nanocarrier can be used to systematically link together different modular components. For example, the outermost mucoadhesive chitosan shell prolongs nasal residence time and opens epithelial paracellular junctions. Because N2B transport operates as an interconnected cascade, the isolated optimization of a single stage can inadvertently impose physicochemical trade-offs that compromise downstream transport phases (Rassu et al. 2017). This study demonstrated multistage recognizing architecture can orchestrate a sequential triple-targeting cascade. Beyond this simple multifunctional stacking, the cutting edge of multistage engineering has incorporated ‘conditional activation’ to resolve the dilemmas of systemic exposure and off-target interactions. A prominent example includes bio-responsive ferritin nano carrier engineered with protective polypeptide shields via matrix metalloproteinase-2/9 (MMP-2/9)-cleavable linkers (Marrocco et al. 2024). These platforms can maintain rigorous physical shielding within the nasal cavity and the initial fluidic pathways, unshielding the core targeting domains only upon encountering pathological enzyme gradients overexpressed in the tumor microenvironment. These sequential advancements demonstrate that N2B delivery engineering has transitioned from passive multifunctional assembly toward a systematic sequential design paradigm (Rassu et al. 2017; Meng et al. 2018; Marrocco et al. 2024).

Nevertheless, formulation platforms that actively target late-stage transport before final cellular uptake remain rare (Yokel 2020; Yokel 2022). Despite being the critical determinants of clinical efficacy, PVS/CSF-mediated redistribution and parenchymal penetration have largely been addressed only through external physical modalities, such as focused ultrasound (FUS) or magnetic field guidance (Chen et al. 2014; Xi et al. 2015; Ye et al. 2021; Li and Feng 2022). However, lessons from alternative CNS administration routes, such as convection-enhanced delivery (CED) or direct intrathecal injection, suggest that post-epithelial transport is not an uncontrollable, passive diffusion process (Nance et al. 2012; Lonser et al. 2015; Pizzo et al. 2018). Rather, it may represent a tunable bottleneck. CSF influx and glymphatic transport do not occur through linear anatomical conduits. Instead, they constitute a dynamic circulation network governed by physiological and hydrodynamic variables (Iliff et al. 2012, 2013; Mestre et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2025). Therefore, N2B formulation engineering must look beyond the epithelial boundary and capture the three columns of late-stage physiology (Influx, Exchange, and Outflow) as independent formulation design parameters (Figure 12) (Iliff et al. 2012, 2013; Mestre et al. 2018; Proulx 2021).

First, the design of the formulation can leverage hemodynamic drive and influx. Arterial pulsatility driven by cardiac cycles serves as the primary physical engine driving CSF into the perivascular channels (Iliff et al. 2013; Mestre et al. 2018). The dobutamine treatment, artificially amplifying arterial pulsatility, significantly accelerates paravascular CSF influx, whereas unilateral internal carotid artery ligation reduces pulsatility via drastically suppresses flow (Iliff et al. 2013). Secondly, modulating intra-tissue fluid exchange can be applied. For convective fluid to penetrate the dense brain parenchyma, efficient solute exchange between the CSF and ISF is mandatory (Iliff et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2025). Biologically, the expression and polarized localization of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels at the astrocytic endfeet act as the molecular gatekeeper of this exchange (Iliff et al. 2012). Therefore, to maximize this fluid-to-tissue transfer, future co-delivery strategies could incorporate transient modulators of AQP4-dependent CSF-ISF exchange alongside the primary therapeutic cargo, or surface-functionalizing the nanocarrier itself with bio-responsive components designed to engage this perivascular exchange interface (Iliff et al. 2012; Simões et al. 2024). By temporally synchronizing the upregulation of this molecular gatekeeper with the arrival of the formulation in the CSF space, or by allowing the nanocarrier to actively breach the parenchymal gateway upon local contact with the astrocytic endfeet, these approaches enable highly precise, on-demand control over intra-tissue delivery kinetics. Lastly, to sustain continuous convective flow and prevent fluid stagnation, an unobstructed exit pathway is vital. CSF drainage is complexly wired not only to the arachnoid villi but also to perineural spaces, the cribriform plate route surrounding the olfactory nerve, and the nasal/dural lymphatic drainage networks (Proulx 2021; Spera et al. 2023). To address this, future formulations could be engineered to actively lower downstream hydrodynamic resistance. For example, nanocarriers designed for the sequential, spatiotemporal release of mild extracellular matrix-remodeling enzymes or lymphatic vasodilators (e.g. VEGF-C) at the exit sites could improve local obstruction, thereby regulating outflow pressure to ensure uninterrupted, deep-brain convective circulation (Song et al. 2020). Collectively, because CSF influx and glymphatic transport function as a dynamic circulation network responsive to physiological variables, N2B delivery platforms must look beyond static cargo characteristics such as size and charge. Instead, they must actively integrate patient hemodynamics (pulsatility), anatomical alignment (posture and AQP4 gatekeepers), and lymphatic clearance capacity into their core architecture (Iliff et al. 2012, 2013; Mestre et al. 2018; Proulx 2021).

Finally, the surface properties of nanocarriers must be sophisticatedly modified to navigate the brain-specific ECM during parenchymal penetration (Nance et al. 2012; Lau et al. 2013). Beyond hyaluronan, the ECM of brain lesions and tumor microenvironments presents highly dense physical barriers composed of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs), collagens, and tenascin-C (Lau et al. 2013). However, because healthy brain ECM is critical for maintaining neurological homeostasis and synaptic plasticity, indiscriminate enzymatic degradation is prohibited due to severe neurotoxicity risks. Therefore, smart N2B that executes localized, transient matrix-remodeling in response to pathological enzyme gradients can be a highly promising and biocompatible design trajectory. Alternatively, platforms utilizing charge-inversion can be employed to maximize diffusion kinetics across the negatively charged interstitial space. These vectors remain positively charged during epithelial translocation, but transit to a neutral or negative state upon entering the parenchymal interface. This temporary charge shift ensures deep tissue penetration without disrupting structural homeostasis.

A further translational consideration is the harmonization of intranasal administration itself. Clinically approved N2B products are delivered as metered nasal sprays or powder devices engineered for reproducible deposition, whereas preclinical studies rely on heterogeneous techniques, ranging from micropipette instillation into the nostril to catheter placement, frequently under anesthesia and supine positioning that maximize olfactory contact in ways human self-administration cannot replicate (Drath et al. 2025). This mismatch confounds cross-study comparison and inflates apparent delivery efficiency relative to what a clinical device could achieve, since conventional sprays deposit only a small fraction of the dose in the upper nasal region. where olfactory transport occurs. Narrowing this gap will require preclinical protocols to report deposition-relevant parameters, such as administered volume, head position, and the targeted nasal region. Harmonizing these approaches to ensure market viability requires a paradigm shift: future formulations can no longer be developed in isolation from physical device engineering and anatomical considerations. Instead, formulation chemistry must be co-developed with advanced delivery technologies, such as anatomically designed olfactory-targeting devices, breath-actuated dispensers, and human nasal cast benchmarking, early in the preclinical stage (Boyuklieva et al. 2023). By embracing this multidisciplinary convergence from the outset, researchers can bridge the gap between preclinical instillation and clinical reality, improving the odds that a promising nanomedicine successfully reaches the market.

Ultimately, advanced, multistage-aware N2B formulations must exceed their historical role as passive vehicles and evolve into dynamic transport systems capable of sequentially decoding the brain's fluidic pathways and pathological tissue barriers to navigate the CNS landscape intelligently.

N2B delivery platforms cannot serve as universally applicable vehicles across disparate therapeutic modalities (Patel et al. 2022). From small molecule generics to peptides, nucleic acids, gene-editing machinery, and complex biological viral vectors, the intrinsic physicochemical and biological identity of each cargo fundamentally dictates both the type and the hierarchy of the biological barriers that the formulation must overcome. Therefore, alongside multi-stage aware, a cargo-informed design that establishes the inherent properties of the payload as the primary engineering starting point is an indispensable prerequisite.

N2B delivery platform for small molecules should overcome local clearance. The primary pharmacokinetic issue for relatively small, lipophilic molecules is ensuring adequate mucosal solubility and prolonged local residence time (Qian et al. 2014; Rassu et al. 2015; Agrawal et al., 2020; Kali et al. 2024). For these payloads, straightforward physicochemical interventions, such as the utilization of cyclodextrin derivatives for inclusion complexation or responsive in situ gelling matrices, are typically sufficient to yield meaningful improvements in global brain delivery efficiency.

Conversely, peptide and protein therapeutics face immediate enzymatic destruction by the dense repertoire of proteases and peptidases in the nasal mucosa, alongside low paracellular permeability due to their hydrophilicity (Hussain et al. 1985; Sarkar 1992; Aungst 2012; Patel et al. 2022). For intermediate peptides like insulin or oxytocin, chemical interventions must be precisely tailored to neutralize mucosal proteases and transiently modulate the epithelial barrier. Specifically, this is achieved by co-incorporating competitive protease inhibitors, such as bacitracin or amastatin, to shield the labile peptide backbone from enzymatic cleavage (Hussain et al. 1989; O'Hagan et al. 1990). Concurrently, specialized paracellular permeation enhancers including sodium glycocholate or medium-chain fatty acids like sodium caprate are utilized to transiently disrupt and dilate epithelial tight junctions, thereby facilitating passive mucosal transit (Aungst 2012). However, macromolecular proteins such as monoclonal antibodies face a more formidable barrier even after crossing the epithelium. The size-exclusion threshold of the pial-glial interface can be a big challenge during parenchymal entry (Pizzo et al. 2018). These therapeutic antibodies are inherently restricted from undergoing passive paracellular diffusion through the tight interstitial gaps. Consequently, formulation strategies for payload must reroute the transport pathway from a paracellular to a transcellular route. Incorporation of multifunctional targeting motifs, such as transferrin- or lactoferrin-receptor ligands, may support receptor-associated uptake or transcytosis pathways (Hu et al. 2009; Gabold et al. 2023).

Nucleic acid therapeutics, including siRNA, ASOs, and mRNA, present entirely different physicochemical hurdles. As highly polyanionic macromolecules, they are inherently incapable of passively crossing lipid bilayers and are rapidly degraded by ubiquitous nucleases within the nasal and extracellular fluids (Howard et al. 2006; Fihurka et al. 2018). Moreover, the conventional engineering approach of using cationic carriers for electrostatic condensation often leads to severe entrapment within the negatively charged mucus mesh, inducing premature clearance (Cone 2009; Lai et al. 2009; Boegh and Nielsen 2015). Therefore, it would be highly advantageous to structurally encapsulate and shield the payload within advanced lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) or polyplex architectures (Howard et al. 2006; Bazargani et al. 2025; Maniyamgama et al., 2025). Furthermore, PEGylation integrating surface charge-masking for mucus penetration alongside stimuli-responsive mechanisms to trigger endosomal escape within a single platform represents a preferred strategy to maximize overall therapeutic efficacy (Suk et al. 2016; Simões et al. 2024).

CRISPR gene-editing systems, such as Cas9/Cas12 ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) and base/prime editors, present a unique physicochemical bottleneck that conflates the vulnerabilities of both protein and nucleic acid payloads (Simões et al. 2024). A fully assembled RNP complex, comprising guide RNA (gRNA) and the Cas protein, is a ~150–200 kDa of macromolecular complex characterized by a highly polyanionic charge and inherent immunogenicity. When utilizing non-viral polymeric or lipidic nanocarriers to condense these systems, researchers face dual constraints that hinder efficient transport. First, charge over-compensation frequently leads to premature entrapment within the negatively charged mucus network (Cone 2009; Lai et al. 2009; Boegh and Nielsen 2015). Subsequently, the payload's bulkiness induces severe steric exclusion by the pial-glial interface and parenchymal ECM (Nance et al. 2012; Pizzo et al. 2018). Consequently, cargo-informed CRISPR platform relies on structural concealing during mucosal and fluidic transit. Further, this carrier must be programmed with multi-stage stimuli-responsive components that trigger rapid endosomal escape and subsequent nuclear localization immediately upon target-cell internalization, maximizing gene-editing efficiency without inducing cellular toxicity (Simões et al. 2024).

Engineered viral vectors, encompassing a wide range of gene therapy vehicles and oncolytic viruses, represent the peak of formulation complexity (Quinn et al. 2011; Gadenstaetter et al. 2022; Zhao et al. 2025). These biological entities present unique engineering challenges based on their distinct physical dimensions. On one end of the physical continuum, small, non-enveloped vectors such as adeno-associated viruses (AAVs, ~25–30 nm) possess rigid capsids that sit near the upper cut-off threshold of glymphatic convective channels (Quinn et al. 2011; Gadenstaetter et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2025), allowing for relatively favorable fluidic transport. Conversely, larger viral vectors, ranging from intermediate enveloped particles like lentiviruses (~80–120 nm) to macroscopic oncolytic platforms including adenoviruses, vaccinia viruses, and herpes simplex viruses (HSVs, up to ~200 nm), suffer severe steric entrapment and immobilization within the dense interstitial mesh of the brain parenchyma (Nance et al. 2012; Yokel 2022; Zhao et al. 2025). Further, all viral modalities share the dual biological vulnerabilities of pronounced systemic immunogenicity and pre-existing host neutralizing antibodies (Quinn et al. 2011; Gadenstaetter et al. 2022), alongside an evolutionarily determined native tissue tropism that often misdirects the cargo away from the intended CNS lesion (Gadenstaetter et al. 2022). Consequently, when designing hybrid biopolymer coatings or supramolecular shielding envelopes to guide these diverse viral entities, core engineering objective is achieving a programmable dynamic equilibrium. The N2B formulation for viral vectors must comprehensively coat the vector's surface capsids or envelopes to evade immunological surveillance during mucosal and fluidic transit, yet seamlessly de-shield at the target site to fully restore the virus's native infectivity, membrane fusion, and cellular transduction capabilities (Quinn et al. 2011; Gadenstaetter et al. 2022).
Ultimately, the refinement of cargo-informed design can be achieved only when formulation engineering fully understands the mechanistic vulnerabilities of a payload (Table 7).

Another critical blind spot in current N2B delivery research is that most formulation platforms are developed and evaluated based on normal physiological barriers under homeostatic conditions (Yokel 2022; Drath et al. 2025; Park and Riew 2025). However, CNS disorders do not preserve static anatomy or physiological states. These are progressive pathologies that continuously remodel the physical, hydrodynamic, and biochemical barriers along the transport pathway over time (Kress et al. 2014; Rasmussen et al. 2018). To achieve successful clinical translation, formulation engineering must exceed the traditional view of anatomy as a static filter. Instead, a paradigm shift toward a ‘disease-informed design’ is required, wherein pathologically induced barrier dynamics are integrated as core variables in N2B formulation engineering (Figure 13).

The very first gate, the nasal mucosa, is profoundly altered by pathological states (Gizurarson 1993; Merkus et al. 1998; Min et al. 2015). In patients with chronic neurodegenerative diseases, systemic neuroinflammation or aging-associated comorbidities often impair MCC and drastically alter intranasal pH and mucus rheology (Gizurarson 1993; Merkus et al. 1998). Under chronic inflammatory conditions, epithelial tight junctions may already be compromised, and altered concentrations of inflammatory proteins in the disease-induced mucus can abnormally amplify non-specific binding with cationic nanocarriers (Cone 2009; Lai et al. 2009; Boegh and Nielsen 2015; Min et al. 2015). In such a pathological environment, mucoadhesive formulations designed for healthy mucosal surfaces may cause excessive aggregation, which ironically impedes epithelial transmigration.

Following epithelial translocation, the hydrodynamic transport pathway undergoes the most dramatic remodeling. While CSF convection and glymphatic perivascular transport are critical drivers of post-epithelial N2B redistribution, these pathways are severely compromised in aging and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) (Kress et al. 2014; Rasmussen et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2025). The loss of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) polarization at the perivascular astroglial foot processes, coupled with diminished arterial pulsatility, weakens the hydrodynamic drivers that support solute movement toward the brain parenchyma (Iliff et al. 2013; Kress et al. 2014; Mestre et al. 2018). Consequently, formulations designed for fluid-mediated targeting that perform well under intact physiological conditions can often fail to reach deep tissues when used in actual disease states. Therefore, formulations targeting late-stage neurodegeneration need to consider to incorporate active mechanisms, such as self-propelled nanomotor systems or transient glymphatic rejuvenators, to autonomously overcome or bypass damaged perivascular spaces (Rasmussen et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2025).

Furthermore, the microenvironment within the brain parenchyma is radically reorganized depending on the disease type and stage, creating a pivotal limitation for final tissue penetration. In malignant brain tumors like glioblastoma (GBM), abnormal neovascularization causes structural disruption of the BBB, leading to a leaky endothelium (Jain et al. 2007). While this hyperpermeability is advantageous for systemic intravenous delivery, it can be a formidable hydrodynamic barrier for N2B delivery. The continuous leakage of intravascular fluid and proteins into the tumor interstitium increases the interstitial fluid pressure (IFP) within the tumor microenvironment. This localized high-pressure environment functions as an outward fluidic barrier, physically repelling N2B cargoes attempting to diffuse into the tumor core from the surrounding CSF space or healthy parenchymal margins.

Simultaneously, pathological progression densely remodels the ECM, the structural scaffold of the brain parenchyma (Syková and Nicholson 2008; Sofroniew 2009; Lau et al. 2013). In ischemic stroke, traumatic brain injury (TBI), or zones of severe neuroinflammation, reactive astrocytes, together with microglial and inflammatory components, contribute to glial scar formation (Sofroniew 2009; Lau et al. 2013). This process involves the excessive deposition of inhibitory components, such as chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) and collagens, which drastically constricts the interstitial mesh size and alters local electrostatic properties (Syková and Nicholson 2008; Sofroniew 2009). Similarly, in neurodegenerative pathologies, the accumulation of amyloid plaques or abnormal protein aggregates introduces massive steric hindrance within the interstitial space (Iliff et al. 2012; Zhang et al. 2023). Ultimately, nanocarriers that exhibit ideal mobility in vitro may lose motility and become entrapped when confronting a fibrotic, pressurized lesion matrix (Syková and Nicholson 2008; Nance et al. 2012).

Taken together, a multistage-aware formulation must be coupled with a disease-informed design to ensure clinical efficacy. From the earliest stages of development, researchers must consider the altered states of the nasal, fluidic, and parenchymal barriers within the specific pathological window of the target disease. Furthermore, in vitro and in vivo validation frameworks must recapitulate microenvironmental pressures and biochemical remodeling. Only by redefining evaluation criteria from absolute bioavailability to lesion-specific target occupancy can N2B platforms evolve into viable clinical modalities.

To date, many studies have relied on bulk, non-fractionated tissue readouts, such as whole-brain fluorescence imaging and total tissue homogenate assays, as proof of delivery success (Ahmad et al. 2017; Yokel 2020; Yokel 2022). Crucially, however, these compartment-blind metrics fail to reflect whether a vehicle is sequestered within intermediate boundary compartments, prematurely disrupted by pathological matrix forces, or rendered non-functional despite structural entry. Therefore, conventional readouts with a single quantitative value can create a general illusion of success that overestimates therapeutically relevant delivery. This methodological overestimation stems from three critical blind spots.

First, bulk readouts can obscure sub-anatomical compartment localization. Even when a robust brain signal or imaging is observed, it cannot discern whether the formulation has penetrated the deep brain parenchyma or remains sequestered within intermediate boundary compartments. As shown by Lochhead et al., intranasal tracers exploit the PVS as a low-resistance convective highway for rapid, brain-wide redistribution (Lochhead et al. 2015). However, while this glymphatic-associated transit is a vital macro-transport pathway, a widespread perivascular signal must not be conflated with widespread parenchymal entry. Without high-resolution confocal or sheet-illumination microscopy to verify paracellular extravasation out of the PVS and into the deep interstitial space, bulk readouts can lead to a misinterpretation of a vehicle on the vascular periphery as a successfully delivered therapeutic.

Secondly, conventional readouts often fail to address the carrier-cargo dissociation during the delivery process. As demonstrated by Ahmad et al. in intranasal nanoemulsion studies, a therapeutic payload can undergo rapid premature leakage or phase separation prior to reaching target sites, migrating through the tissue independently of its delivery vehicle (Ahmad et al. 2017). Consequently, observing a fluorescently labeled cargo within brain sections does not automatically imply the successful post-entry transport of an intact nanocarrier. To dismantle this illusion, future frameworks must implement dual-labeling strategies or advanced biophysical assays, such as Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET), to differentiate between the signal of a structurally cohesive platform and that of a liberated, naked cargo (Ahmad et al. 2017; Yokel 2020).

Lastly, the physical accumulation of formulation within the brain does not warrant functional intracellular uptake or biological activation of therapeutics. Whether the delivered cargo undergoes productive target-cell penetration, endosomal escape, and pharmacological interaction remains an entirely separate biological hurdle. Therefore, experiments that directly assay cargo functionality provide more rigorous evidence of late-stage delivery success than simple fluorescent tracking (Harmon et al. 2014; Aly et al. 2023). For instance, Harmon et al. demonstrated functionally effective delivery by confirming that intranasally administered CK30PEG-compacted plasmid DNA nanoparticles successfully drove downstream eGFP expression in rat brains (Harmon et al. 2014). Similarly, Aly et al. showed that intranasal delivery of mutant huntingtin-lowering ASO-loaded apoA-I nanodiscs reduced toxic huntingtin protein levels in the cortex and striatum (Aly et al. 2023).

To address these limitations, future N2B studies should adopt a stage-resolved validation framework aligned with the transport cascade defined in Section 2. Each experimental setting should be matched to the specific stage it intends to support. In this framework, a whole-brain signal should be treated only as an initial screening endpoint, whereas claims of meaningful delivery require additional evidence of carrier integrity, compartment-resolved localization, true parenchymal entry, and functional target engagement. The recommended minimum and advanced validation criteria for each transport stage are summarized in Table 8.

While the stage-resolved framework is most informative when tailored to a given transport step, not every criterion applies to every formulation, so a minimal set of stage-agnostic requirements is useful as a common baseline that any N2B study should satisfy. First, direct nose-to-brain transport should be distinguished from systemic recirculation, for example by comparing intranasal with intravenous or a matched parenteral route and reporting a drug-targeting efficiency or direct-transport percentage rather than brain signal alone. Second, quantification must be normalized to the administered dose and be compartment-specific. Rather than analyzing whole-brain bulk homogenates, studies should use perfusion or tissue fractionation to distinguish actual brain tissue (parenchyma) from blood vessels and cerebrospinal fluid. Third, carrier and cargo should be tracked as distinct entities, so that measured brain signal reflects the intended species rather than a dissociated label or free payload. Finally, delivery should be linked to a functional or pharmacodynamic readout that confirms the cargo reaches its site of action in an active form. These four requirements, namely route-controlled transport, normalized compartment-aware quantification, carrier-cargo discrimination, and functional confirmation, are applicable regardless of carrier chemistry and provide a comparable foundation onto which stage-specific validation can be layered.

On the other hand, the anatomical divergence between the rodent models and human nasal anatomy should be considered a translational constraint. As emphasized by Yokel the olfactory epithelium covers approximately 41%–52% of the nasal cavity surface in adult rats, whereas in humans it occupies only approximately 3.0%–10.5% (Yokel 2022). Unlike small molecules, for cargoes larger than 100 nm, only a small fraction is expected to deposit in the human olfactory region, making direct comparisons with rodent instillation studies complicated. This discrepancy is further amplified by common rodent protocols, in which formulations are often instilled under anesthesia and supine positioning, thereby increasing olfactory epithelial contact under conditions that do not reflect human self-administration. These anatomical and procedural disparities argue for complementing rodent efficacy data with human nasal cast deposition studies, primary human nasal epithelial cell air‒liquid interface models, and large-animal nasal deposition models such as porcine or ovine systems.

Beyond these deposition-focused surrogates, nonhuman primate (NHP) models provide the closest approximation to human nasal physiology, since the olfactory region of macaques occupies a proportion of the nasal cavity comparable to that of humans and is similarly sequestered from the main airstream, allowing spray deposition, olfactory targeting, and systemic clearance to be evaluated under near-human geometry (Lee et al. 2020). Intranasal delivery of macromolecules and peptides to the primate CNS along olfactory and trigeminal pathways has been demonstrated on this basis, supporting the translational relevance of NHP data for deposition and transport (Sasaki et al. 2023). Human-derived three-dimensional systems, including nasal organoids and nose-on-a-chip platforms, provide a complementary but fundamentally different capability. These microphysiological models can recapitulate cell-level features such as epithelial barrier integrity, mucus turnover, and paracellular permeability that are difficult to control in vivo, yet they do not reproduce the macroscopic airflow, regional deposition, and whole-axis fluid transport that define the rodent-human anatomical gap in the first place. Their value therefore lies in dissecting stage-specific cellular mechanisms rather than in resolving the geometric and hydrodynamic discrepancies of the intact nasal pathway, for which in vivo NHP models remain indispensable.

In summary, although a whole-brain signal can serve as a useful experimental starting point, it is insufficient to confirm deep parenchymal penetration or productive target-cell engagement. The primary limitation of current N2B validation is the lack of stage-specific evidence capable of decoupling post-entry redistribution from true intra-tissue diffusion, carrier integrity, and functional uptake. Therefore, future N2B studies should move beyond the binary paradigm of total brain readout and adopt validation frameworks that verify vehicle integrity, compartment-resolved localization, parenchymal penetration, and functional target engagement in a stage-resolved manner (Harmon et al. 2014; Lochhead et al. 2015; Yokel 2020; Aly et al. 2023).

The current translational stagnation in N2B delivery is caused, in part, by a profound conceptual oversimplification. N2B transport is a formidable, sequential cascade encompassing mucosal retention, epithelial translocation, fluidic redistribution, and deep intraparenchymal extracellular diffusion. To bridge this translational gap, formulation engineering must shift toward an integrated paradigm built on three core principles. Future formulations must actively orchestrate multistage-aware designs to spatiotemporally harmonize sequential functionalities, cargo-informed architectures tailored to the payload's distinct vulnerabilities, and disease-informed approaches capable of adapting to pathologically remodeled physical and hydrodynamic barriers. Ultimately, even the most advanced delivery platforms will fail to achieve clinical maturity without a rigorous, stage-resolved validation framework. We recommend the adoption of compartment-resolved imaging, FRET-based dissociation assays, and functional readouts to explicitly decouple passive fluidic distribution from true parenchymal penetration and functional execution. Furthermore, recognizing the profound anatomical discrepancies in olfactory surface area between preclinical rodent models and humans is paramount. Equally important, the biofate, clearance, and long-term safety of these systems must be characterized alongside efficacy, since regulatory translation depends as much on how a carrier is eliminated from the brain as on how it is delivered. By integrating human-relevant anatomical evaluation models and strictly enforcing stage-specific validation, N2B delivery can move beyond its status as a preclinical phenomenon and evolve into a reliable, transformative clinical modality for CNS therapeutics.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: Bottlenecks at the nasal deposition and retention stage. Four sequential barriers restrict therapeutic cargo from reaching the olfactory epithelium. 1) An aerodynamic bottleneck is imposed by the anterior nasal geometry. 2) A physical bottleneck arises from charge- and size-mediated drug entrapment within the mucus network. 3) A mucociliary bottleneck is driven by rapid mucociliary clearance (MCC). 4) A biochemical bottleneck results from local immunoglobulin A (IgA), hydrolytic enzymes, and low pH that promote early cargo degradation and inactivation. These compounded early-stage losses determine the functionally available fraction of the administered dose that can advance to epithelial crossing. Created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Figure 2.
figures.caption: Overview of the three primary nasal epithelial crossing routes. The paracellular route and perineural bulk flow achieve central nervous system (CNS) exposure within seconds to minutes. Epithelial transcytosis operates on a timescale of 10 minutes to hours. Intraneuronal axonal transport requires hours to days. This timescale hierarchy determines which route governs the rapid initial CNS signal versus sustained cargo distribution. The mechanistic bottlenecks and cargo requirements for each route are summarized in Table 1. Created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: Anatomical trajectories and stage-specific bottlenecks of the olfactory and trigeminal routes. Along the olfactory route, cargo migrates alongside olfactory nerve bundles through the cribriform plate toward the subarachnoid space (SAS) and olfactory bulb, encountering three principal bottlenecks: 1) a restricted physical bottleneck at the densely packed cribriform plate foramina and 2) a slow transport timescale for intraneuronal axonal transit. Along the trigeminal route, cargo migrates through perineuronal spaces of the trigeminal nerve (V) toward the brainstem and cerebellum via the SAS, encountering two bottlenecks: 1) a long transport axis from the nasal cavity to the posterior CNS, 2) fluidic resistance within the perineuronal space (PNS), and 3) a slow transport timescale for perineural transit. The olfactory route preferentially targets anterior CNS structures via cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-mediated redistribution, whereas the trigeminal route provides a conduit to the posterior and inferior CNS regions. Created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: Bidirectional fluid dynamics at the CNS fluid-tissue interface. Schematic depicting the two opposing fluid exchange processes governing cargo redistribution between CNS fluid compartments and the brain parenchyma: cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) influx into the parenchyma and interstitial fluid (ISF) outflux into the subarachnoid space (SAS). The balance and directionality of these fluidic processes determine whether cargo that has entered the CSF or perivascular space (PVS) toward the deeper parenchyma or is diverted toward clearance pathways. Created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Figure 5.
figures.caption: Structural barriers to intraparenchymal penetration at the fluid-tissue interface. Two biophysical obstacles restrict cargo from advancing from the perivascular space (PVS) into the brain parenchyma: 1) a size-exclusion filter imposed by the cellular and matrix architecture at the fluid-tissue interface, and 2) a dense extracellular matrix (ECM) composed of hyaluronan (HA), proteoglycans, tenascin, fibronectin, and collagen and elastic fibers that restricts intraparenchymal diffusion through steric hindrance. Astrocytes, fibroblasts, and blood vessels are depicted in their spatial arrangement at the PVS-parenchyma boundary, and ISF influx from the PVS into the parenchymal interstitium is indicated. Created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Figure 6.
figures.caption: Five cellular-level barriers at the target-cell engagement stage. Even after intraparenchymal accumulation, therapeutic cargo must overcome the following sequential barriers: 1) non-specific membrane interactions that divert cargo from the intended receptor-bearing target cell, 2) competition with endogenous substances for binding at neuron-specific receptors, 3) intracellular enzymatic degradation and inactivation following uptake, 4) endolysosomal sequestration driven by lysosomal enzyme activity, and 5) restricted nuclear localization for gene-active payloads. These five barriers collectively define target-cell engagement as a distinct functional endpoint that cannot be inferred from parenchymal accumulation data alone. Created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Figure 7.
figures.caption: Physical interventions in the early nasal stage. Standard nasal sprays deposit over 90% of the dose in the anterior cavity, with typically less than 1% reaching the olfactory region. Anatomically targeted deposition is improved by optimizing administration angle and plume geometry or by using breath-actuated bidirectional devices, which increase posterior deposition approximately three-fold. Local residence is then engineered through in situ gelling, mucoadhesive polymers such as chitosan and hyaluronic acid, and mucus-penetrating systems including PEGylated micelles and cyclodextrin inclusion complexes. Together, anatomically targeted deposition and residence engineering maximize the fraction available for subsequent epithelial crossing. MCC, mucociliary clearance. PEG, polyethylene glycol. Created with Manus.

figures.label: Figure 8.
figures.caption: Biochemical and immunological interventions at the nasal interface. Retained cargo must remain biologically intact and transport-competent against proteolytic degradation, nuclease-mediated degradation, and immune recognition. Enzymatic protection through protease inhibition or nanocarrier encapsulation extends the window for productive epithelial transport, as illustrated by naked DNA degrading within approximately 20 minutes while nanoparticle-encapsulated DNA remains largely preserved. Responsive dissociation uses local biochemical cues, such as the mildly acidic nasal pH, to trigger carrier-cargo separation and release at the mucosal interface. Reduced immunological exposure through vector or serotype selection and surface shielding preserves vector activity before target-site entry. Created with BioRender.com and Manus.

figures.label: Figure 9.
figures.caption: Engineering nasal epithelial crossing. Epithelial crossing converts surface exposure into true tissue entry, with tight junctions restricting paracellular passage and macromolecules requiring active transcellular transport or barrier modulation. Paracellular modulation transiently and reversibly loosens tight junctions, for example through quaternized chitosan that remains active near neutral pH. Matrix or barrier remodeling by enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) or hyaluronidase may facilitate post-epithelial tissue penetration. Transcellular uptake and cargo protection require apical uptake, intracellular survival and trafficking, and basolateral release, supported by cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) and receptor-targeting ligands. Created with Manus.

figures.label: Figure 10.
figures.caption: Implemented strategies for post-epithelial N2B redistribution. After epithelial crossing, cargo repartitions among perineural spaces, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), subarachnoid space (SAS), perivascular space (PVS), and clearance routes, such that fluid-space exposure does not equate to parenchymal delivery. Adjunct approaches include pharmacological modulation that reduces CSF turnover to increase drug retention, magnetic guidance and focused ultrasound to overcome local hydrodynamic resistance, and ultrasmall biomimetic nanodiscs that reduce ECM steric trapping and support functional neural delivery. A key interpretation gap remains, as CSF or PVS signal is not equivalent to confirmed parenchymal delivery and requires compartment-resolved localization, boundary crossing, deep-tissue distribution, and functional target engagement. Direct carrier-intrinsic control of post-epithelial pathways remains limited relative to device-assisted strategies. SAS, subarachnoid space. PVS, perivascular space. ECM, extracellular matrix. SPION, superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticle. ASO, antisense oligonucleotide. Created with Manus.

figures.label: Figure 11.
figures.caption: Cellular internalization and functional delivery. Successful delivery is defined by engagement of the therapeutically relevant target rather than by brain signal alone, so the required endpoint depends on where the target is located. Receptor-mediated targeting biases cargo toward disease-relevant cells through receptor-ligand interactions, such as H-ferritin with transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) or lactoferrin with its receptor. Membrane penetration and biological tropism enhance local cellular access through cell-penetrating peptides, exosomal tropism, or cell-based shuttles. Conditional activation uses disease-associated cues, including pH, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and proteases, to spatially unmask targeting or activate cargo release, whereas extracellular target engagement can define successful delivery without cellular entry. TfR1, transferrin receptor 1. LfR, lactoferrin receptor. MMP, matrix metalloproteinase. Created with Manus.

figures.label: Figure 12.
figures.caption: Conceptual framework for multistage-aware N2B formulation design. The framework organizes N2B engineering into four sequentially addressed phases. Phase 1 (nasal entry) addresses the balance between nasal residence and mucus penetration, cargo protection from pH, enzymatic, and immune exposure, and the incorporation of epithelial-opening or transcytosis-enabling modules. Phase 2 (fluidic pathways) treats CSF, SAS, and PVS as active, tunable bottlenecks, targeting influx modulation, CSF-ISF exchange via aquaporin-4 (AQP4), and outflow resistance. Phase 3 (parenchymal penetration) focuses on crossing the pial-glia limitans and ECM barriers through surface passivation, charge inversion, or localized matrix remodeling. Phase 4 (target-cell engagement) requires cargo integrity preservation until cell contact, conditional activation at the lesion site, and direct verification of uptake, endosomal escape, and functional response. A representative sequential modular carrier integrating a chitosan shell, lipid shield, and RVG-9R functional core is shown as an example of multistage integration. CSF, cerebrospinal fluid. SAS, subarachnoid space. PVS, perivascular space. ECM, extracellular matrix. MMP, matrix metalloproteinase. RVG, rabies virus glycoprotein. Created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Figure 13.
figures.caption: Integrated cargo-informed and disease-informed design framework for N2B delivery. Left panel (Cargo-informed design): Formulation strategies must scale with payload complexity. Small molecules require solubility and residence enhancement; peptides/proteins need protease protection and permeation enhancers (with mAbs requiring receptor-mediated transport). CRISPR and viral vectors demand advanced encapsulation (LNP/polyplex), charge shielding, endosomal escape, and dynamic de-shielding at target sites. Right panel (Disease-informed design): Biological barriers dynamically remodel with disease progression. While normal physiology serves as baseline control, early-stage pathologies exhibit altered mucus, MCC, and impaired glymphatic exchange. Late-stage conditions introduce high interstitial fluid pressure (IFP), dense ECM (glial scars), and steric trapping by protein plaques. Ultimately, formulations must be tailored to the specific disease stage and validated for lesion-specific target occupancy.
